#6411. The Best Little Gifts Your Holiday Party Host Will Actually Want

Don’t show up empty-handed or with a cheap bottle of wine — bring status cocktail cherries, a beeswax candle, or a painterly placemat

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

A good host is always thinking of others, whether it’s by making guests feel welcome, accommodating everyone’s diets, or setting an Instagram-worthy tablescape to make the night feel extra special. But the holiday season is an opportunity to flip the script and show the host you’re thinking of them, too. Bringing them a gift is the cardinal way to thank the host for all their thoughtful work. The only question remains: what to give?

For those who delight in trotting out their special dinnerware for guests, there’s a world of creative and whimsical gifts out there, even if it seems like they already have the entire CB2 catalog. And if that is the case, this just means you, as the gift-giver, can allow them to indulge in the things they typically would not. Take, for instance, some unique vintage shot glasses, intricately carved chopsticks, and pearl cocktail picks. Not only do these playful takes on essentials inspire joy, but they’re also sure to be conversation starters for future gatherings. And, as the bestower of the new treasured piece, you just might secure yourself the invite for the next one.

You can never have enough serving utensils if you love to host. That moment when you toss your pasta salad, plate everyone’s green beans, or dole out your main dish is an opportunity to flex some of your more decorative yet functional kitchen tools. This ethereal stainless steel set from Leif boasts pewter star-shaped handles with sea glass.

Even Diaspora Spice Co.’s everyday spices come in bold, ready-to-gift packaging, but the equitable spice company’s new holiday spice sampler gift box is an extra colorful treat for the senses. The bundle includes samples of its beloved Nandini coriander, a rare Ceylon cinnamon, a Himalayan foothills-sourced pink garlic powder, and several more spices to inspire your host.

When it comes to gift-giving, we believe in working smarter, not harder. Case in point: Buy a set of nice-looking vintage glasses — these are labeled shot glasses by the seller, but they’re just as nice for sipping cordials — and rather than giving one lovely host a set of eight, split them up into pairs or fours and use them for multiple gifting situations. There’s always a use for little glasses like this (and they’re pretty enough to display, too).

It’s pretty fun to use a posh plaid napkin when you’re digging into some quiche or sipping on mulled wine.

It’s always fun to kick off an evening of cocktails with a caviar bump, which is what makes this Imperia Caviar bundle such a gift for the avid party host. The 30-gram tin of royal ossetra comes with a mother-of-pearl spoon and a caviar tin opener in a velvet bag, and the bundle’s compact size means you can simply slide it into your purse or jacket on the way to the function (unlike a heavy bottle of wine or olive oil, which would likely need their owns bags).

It really has been the year of the dirty martini. For those who are building a bar cart (or want to start), getting a couple of sets of proper cocktail picks can be a game-changer. Nothing wrong with a traditional wood toothpick, of course, but it really does add a lot of pizzazz to a martini to bite the olives off a pearl-emblazoned skewer.

Swooning will abound once people get a look at these beautiful walnut chopsticks featuring inlaid geometric designs. Another great example of “practical, but nicer to look at than what you might get for yourself.” Plus, you can grab a set of five on sale right now for under $20.

When it comes to cocktail cherries, one brand truly reigns supreme: Luxardo, which has been making candied cherries soaked in marasca syrup for 120 years. A classic for a reason!

Jonathan Adler is another designer to keep tabs on when it comes to playful but elevated home decor. This set of Matisse-esque coasters also has a slight lip to keep condensation from spilling, and would be prime for serving up lychee martinis the next time you gather with friends. Snag them while they’re 40% off for Black Friday.

Halen Môn is a salt nerd’s dream. The organic, hand-harvested sea salt hails from the tides of the Isle of Anglesey in Wales (Halen is Welsh for salt; Môn is Welsh for Anglesey), and has earned numerous awards for its subtle crunch and crisp mineral flavor. Any host would be thrilled to receive a bag of the stuff, but this gift set combines the salt with a charming ceramic cellar and spoon.

Matches are always a solid host gift, and a small but useful present that’s made all the better with cool packaging. The lifestyle brand State the Label, for example, has housed its matches in a folk art-inspired cottage (the striker paper is on the bottom of the house).

Those who like to entertain likely appreciate a good placemat. This set of two block-printed placemats from West Elm puts a romantic spin on the dining-table staple with painterly tones and bright hues. Who wouldn’t love to receive these dreamy accents?

Is your host a lover of ice-cold martinis? Perfect gift incoming: Quincy’s fabulous olives, which have superb flavor and are ratioed with drink-perfect brine to make exactly 14 dirty martinis per jar.

Scents are tricky. Unless you really know your host, refrain from gifting them scented candles, and opt for a beeswax pillar candle instead; they can light it sans candelabra (unless you’re sure that they own one and prefer tapers) by simply placing it on a small plate. Above all, beeswax candles make a wonderful dining companion, because they don’t emit the same stuffy, paraffin wax-based smoke as non-beeswax candles.

Sometimes, brevity is wit. Give it to someone who means business, or orders the business women special.

We all love a little Le Creuset in our kitchens, but a Dutch oven isn’t in the price range for what we’d consider an easy host gift. Enter the butter dish, a fabulous little thing to present and say “I brought you something,” presented with a kiss on the cheek and maybe a bouquet of flowers or bottle of wine.

#6410. Earth’s Lakes Are Changing in Unison – and Scientists Are Worried

Lakes play an important role in regulating Earth’s carbon cycle, and scientists warn that environmental changes occurring across many lakes at once could amplify global climate risks.

Lakes around the world are increasingly changing in step, a trend that could weaken a natural buffer against environmental disruption. A new study found that this synchronization has accelerated markedly since 2000.

The characteristics of a lake’s watershed, the land that drains into it, have historically helped buffer its ecosystem against broader environmental changes. Lakes fluctuated independently, a pattern known as “spatial asynchrony” that spread ecological disturbances across time and space.

A team led by Prof. Ke Zhang of the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (NIGLAS) combined century-scale sediment records with continuous satellite observations from approximately 2,000 lakes. Alongside growing synchrony, the researchers found a significant decline in network modularity, meaning the lake network was becoming less divided into groups with distinct patterns of change.

The researchers used water clarity and phytoplankton biomass, the mass of microscopic organisms that use sunlight to make food, as proxies for lake metabolic activity. These indicators provide an indirect view of how lake ecosystems process energy and nutrients. Their growing synchrony suggests that the underlying carbon, nutrient, and biodiversity dynamics they reflect may also be becoming more synchronized.

The study attributes this shift to environmental telecoupling, connections through which climate extremes such as heatwaves and socioeconomic pressures link changes across distant regions. The authors describe this increasingly linked response to large-scale environmental change as a new hallmark of the Anthropocene, a term used to describe a world profoundly shaped by human activity.

Although lakes cover less than 2% of Earth’s surface, they help regulate global carbon and nutrient cycles and biodiversity. Losing the differences in how they respond to environmental pressures could therefore have consequences well beyond individual watersheds.

“This loss of buffering capacity transforms lakes from passive, regionally distinct systems into active amplifiers of global environmental risks. Synchronized lakes can concentrate biophysical fluxes, potentially triggering high-amplitude global pulses, such as simultaneous greenhouse gas emissions or widespread aquatic hypoxia, thereby exacerbating the triple planetary crisis,” Zhang said.

Aquatic hypoxia means a shortage of oxygen in the water. The “triple planetary crisis” refers to climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution.

Water management has traditionally treated lakes as isolated local resources, creating what the researchers describe as a “scale mismatch” between governance and the processes shaping these ecosystems. Zhang and his co-authors propose treating interconnected lake networks as a dynamically coupled “Planetary Commons.” Their objective is to protect the local ecological processes that maintain variation across landscapes, without seeking to eliminate synchrony.

To put that idea into practice, the team introduced a framework called Strategic Planetary Lake Areas (SPLAs). By tracking large-scale measures of synchrony and modularity, policymakers could identify priority regions, including regional groups of lakes whose behavior is rapidly converging. These areas could become candidates for targeted polycentric governance, an approach involving multiple centers of decision-making.

“This research not only redefines the critical importance of inland waters in global change studies but also introduces a macroscale dimension to international sustainable development agendas,” Zhang said. “The work emphasizes that preserving the diversity of ecological responses is essential for maintaining long-term Earth-system stability in an increasingly interconnected world.”

Reference: “Global lake synchrony signals rising planetary-scale ecological coupling” by Ke Zhang, Yaoyao Han, Lindsey Gillson, Xiaoling Zhang, Suzanne McGowan, Michael E. Meadows, Yuan Jin, Luki Subehi, John A. Dearing, David P. Hamilton, Yan Zhao, Lian Pin Koh and David Taylor, 16 November 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2611874123

“The authors describe this increasingly linked response to large-scale environmental change as a new hallmark of the Anthropocene.”

The article doesn’t really support their claim of “increasing synchrony.” This sounds more like assigning a scapegoat than explaining what is driving the alleged changes. It appears to me that the relationship is best described by a U-shaped function rather than a linear, long-term trend. The index graph that is most U-like is the one going back farthest in time, suggesting some periodicity related to time.

The R^2 value in all cases is less than 0.5, and in most cases less than 0.2. That means that the variance in the dependent variable that is explained by the changes in the independent variable is less than the probability of getting a ‘Head’ in a coin flip. That doesn’t convince me that they really understand what is going on. But the buzzword salad had all the right words and conclusions to get published!

The brains of people with PTSD bear molecular changes that differ from those in people with other conditions, like depression, a new study finds.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A study of hundreds of brains has revealed molecular differences in people with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) that are not found in individuals without the condition.

These molecular marks also differ from those seen in the brains of people with other conditions, like depression, the research found.

Our environment and experiences influence how our genes work, affecting which genes can be turned on. Rather than changing genes' underlying code, the environment can trigger what are known as epigenetic changes, which include certain chemicals that attach to DNA molecules and change their structure.

One such epigenetic change, called methylation, can work like a "dimmer switch" for genes, or even completely block certain genes from turning on.

"These epigenetic features of the brain are important for shaping the way the brain functions," study co-author Frances Champagne, a psychologist at the University of Texas at Austin, told Live Science. "This can give us some insight into why individuals with PTSD develop PTSD, or how [their brains] are different from a healthy brain."

In the new study, published Friday (Nov. 20) in the journal Cell Reports, scientists took a close look at DNA methylation in 302 brains that had been donated after death. These included 101 brains from individuals diagnosed with PTSD, 101 from people with major depressive disorder and 100 from people without any diagnosed psychiatric disorders. The researchers also had access to these individuals' medical records.

The team zoomed in on three brain regions: the prefrontal cortex, the amygdala and the hippocampus. The prefrontal cortex handles cognitive functions like planning and decision-making, the amygdala is a major hub for emotional processing, and the hippocampus is key for memory and learning.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"The goal of our study was to look at the epigenetics of the PTSD brain and ask how [it] is different from that of an individual who does not have PTSD," Champagne said, "or who comparatively has another diagnosis, like major depressive disorder."

Compared to the brains of people without any disorders, the brains of people with PTSD had different patterns of methylation in the prefrontal cortex, in particular. By contrast, in major depressive disorder, the amygdala stood out as a brain region with distinct methylation.

Additionally, in depression, the observed differences in methylation tended to affect the same set of genes across different regions of the brain. This was not the case in PTSD, which showed more inconsistencies in terms of which specific genes were involved. The methylation patterns in PTSD also appeared to vary depending on other factors, such as patients' sex, ethnicity and age at which they experienced trauma.

The study's results serve as a valuable resource, said Seyma Katrinli, an investigator in the Grady Trauma Project, a large PTSD study, at the Emory University School of Medicine.

Although the findings can't be used to help diagnose PTSD yet, down the line, this area of research could help scientists correlate changes that are measurable in people's blood to changes in the brain, said Katrinli, who was not involved in the new work. Then, blood tests could help guide the diagnosis and treatment of PTSD, she suggested.

That said, the study had limitations. Because the scientists analyzed postmortem brains, they relied on the medical reports rather than assessing the study subjects directly. Additionally, both PTSD and major depressive disorder are associated with substance use, which also causes DNA methylation; this potential confounding factor was not accounted for in the study. .

Finally, at this point, there is no way to tell what triggered the observed differences in DNA methylation. The scientists can't say if the variations are a consequence of PTSD, a risk factor for PTSD, or a downstream effect of other things that co-occur with PTSD.

The research sets the stage to "help us ask better questions," Champagne said. Her team is now looking to investigate factors — such as sex, the timing of traumatic experiences, or history of substance use — that may be driving the variation within PTSD.

"It's a very exciting foray into epigenetic profiling in the brain," she said.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Wylie, D., Arasappan, D., Ross, D., Hyde, T. M., Ressler, K. J., Kleinman, J. E., Weinberger, D. R., Daskalakis, N. P., Nemeroff, C. B., & Champagne, F. A. (2026). DNA methylation profiling of human brain in posttraumatic stress and major depressive disorders indicate specific molecular features. Cell Reports, 118270. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118270

#6408. Losing Weight but Getting Less Healthy? Study Reveals a Dark Side of Keto

Mice that lost weight on a very low-protein keto diet also developed fatty liver and lost muscle, highlighting the limitations of weight as a measure of health.

Ketogenic diets have become a popular approach to weight loss, despite conflicting research on their metabolic benefits. A new study in mice suggests that two often overlooked factors may help explain these inconsistencies: the amount of protein in the diet and the genetic makeup of the animals eating it. The findings also raise questions about whether losing weight on a keto diet necessarily means becoming healthier.

The research, published in Cell Metabolism, began when first author Zhaoyue Zhang, a postdoctoral fellow in the Friedman lab, noticed considerable variation in the protein content of ketogenic diets. Although these diets are generally high in fat and extremely low in carbohydrates, their protein content could be contributing to differences in metabolic outcomes.

Zhang and her colleagues systematically tested diets containing different proportions of fat and protein. After four weeks on a ketogenic diet containing just 5% protein, mice belonging to C57Bl/6J, the most commonly used laboratory mouse strain, reduced their food intake by approximately 40% and lost weight. Mice fed an otherwise similar diet containing 10% protein ate more and gained weight. Both groups produced ketones, molecules generated when the body relies heavily on fat for fuel, suggesting that ketosis alone could not account for the difference.

“The result was so striking,” Zhang says.

A closer look at the mice that lost weight revealed a more complicated picture. Although their glucose tolerance, or ability to manage changes in blood sugar, improved, they also developed fatty liver. Much of their weight loss was associated with reductions in lean mass, including muscle.

To understand what was suppressing the animals’ appetite, the researchers investigated GDF15, a hormone released in response to cellular stress that can act on the brain to reduce food intake. When they conducted an experiment using genetically modified mice lacking GDF15, even the control mice unexpectedly failed to lose weight on the low-protein diet.

“At first, I was a bit panicked,” Zhang says. “We had repeated the same experiment many times, and all of a sudden it didn’t work.”

Retracing her steps, Zhang discovered that the genetically modified mice belonged to a different substrain, C57Bl/6N, which shares approximately 99.9% of its genome with the mice used in the earlier experiments.

“This realization was key, and it became the starting point for the rest of the study,” Zhang says.

The researchers eventually identified two genes that helped explain the difference: NNT, which protects cells against oxidative stress, and NLRP12, which helps regulate inflammation. The mice susceptible to weight loss, known as B6J, carried mutations in both genes. Feeding them the low-protein ketogenic diet triggered stress and inflammatory responses in the liver, accompanied by rising levels of GDF15 and an inflammation-associated protein called LCN2. Both proteins can influence appetite through their effects on the brain.

Restoring NNT function in B6J mice caused them to eat more and lose less weight. Conversely, disabling both genes in the genetically similar B6NJ mice, which normally carry functioning versions of both genes, caused them to eat less and lose weight. Treatment with N-acetylcysteine, an antioxidant with anti-inflammatory properties, also lowered circulating levels of GDF15 and LCN2, increased food intake, and reduced weight loss.

Zhang cautions that the findings cannot be directly applied to humans, particularly because the 5% protein diet contained substantially less protein than most ketogenic diets used in clinical trials. Future trials could benefit from paying closer attention to both dietary protein content and genetic differences among participants, while looking beyond weight loss and blood sugar control when assessing metabolic health.

The researchers now want to investigate whether other genetic factors influence responses to ketogenic diets and whether the changes they observed can be reversed once the diet is discontinued.

Reference: “Macronutrient composition and genetic background determine the response to a ketogenic diet in mice” by Zhaoyue Zhang, Alexandre Moura-Assis, Shanshan Liu, Alon Millet, Jordan Shaked, Divya Rajan, Katelin Chen, Anduena Toci, Chloe Schaefer, Ijeoma Obi, Sebastian Carrasco, Sandra Kelly Atkinson, Francois Marchildon, Hanan Alwaseem, Michael Isay-Del Viscio, Henrik Molina, Paul Cohen, Kivanc Birsoy and Jeffrey Friedman, 18 November 2026, Cell Metabolism. DOI: 10.1016/j.cmet.2026.10.017

#6407. Robots, Not Astronauts, Will Have to Fix Space Data Centers

Yesterday we explored some of the difficulties facing orbital data centers in our look at the bottleneck of launching enough solar panels and radiative cooling systems to power the AI computing boom in space. JPl physicist Dr. Slava Turyshev, who wrote the paper at the center of that article, also published a follow-up study in August, available in preprint on arXiv, about how getting the hardware off the ground is only half the battle. Once all that equipment is up there, someone, or something, is going to have to maintain it.

Modern hardware powering Artificial Intelligence even on Earth has an obsolescence problem. The computer chips and memory that power AI data centers become obsolete every 3-5 years. If a company builds an orbital data center, its processing power is effectively useless for training the latest AI models in less than half a decade. So, in their business plans, the solution is to build intentionally disposable satellites.

Unfortunately, that means throwing away literal tons of still-useful solar panels and heat radiators just to discard some obsolete computer hardware. Given that those bulkier pieces of equipment pose their own challenge for launches, as we saw yesterday, that seems a bit of a waste. So, Dr. Turyshev suggests that orbital data centers must be designed with hardware replacement in mind.

Fraser talks about a NASA project designed to assemble large-scale structures in space.

On Earth, replacement of data server racks involves a human technician walking down an air-conditioned aisle, pulling some cables, and pressing pins before replacing a standardized blade. In orbit, that would require a pressurized housing with airlocks, life support and fire suppression systems, while still having the problem of cooling all of those heat-producing microchips in the vacuum of space. According to Dr. Turyshev, that means the entire data center architecture should be based around plug-and-play âorbital replacement unitsâ (ORUs).

He assigns each of those ORUs into one of three main replaceable component tiers (alongside replacing an entire 100 kW satellite node if it suffers catastrophic damage). One is a 5 kW âcomputeâ module that holds the memory, storage and optical transceivers necessary to actually perform calculations. These are designed to be rapidly swappable, and are intended to be the most replaced part of the whole satellite.

Another ORU category is the âsubsystemsâ â the power converters, batteries, pumps, and manifolds meant to keep the whole system running but that are settled enough technologically to not require regular replacement. In the paperâs architecture, these can be swapped out by specialized 6 or 7 degree-of-freedom robotic arms, as compared to the automated cartridge changers that handle replacing the compute modules.

Fraser talks about the difficulties repairing missions at L2, like JWST.

The third group of ORUs consists of the solar arrays and radiator panels themselves. Making them modular has the added advantage of not needing to replace the entire cooling or power generation system if one part happens to be struck by a micrometeoroid, which will undoubtedly happen often even in Low Earth Orbit. Despite the fact these modules make up the bulk of the weight and surface area of the spacecraft, they will not have to be repaired as frequently as the compute modules, as random failures caused by cosmic rays will brick compute modules fairly frequently..

Unfortunately, replacing these systems isnât as easy as it would be on Earth. Each 5 kW processor will heat up nearly half a degree Celsius every second, triggering a thermal overload in a little less than a minute if left uncooled. And the power capacitors riding along to maintain power to the system have the capability of producing an arc strong enough to weld a robotic gripper to a maintenance touch point, so they must be bled off before a robot can start interacting with the satelliteâs hardware.

And then, there is once again the sense of scale. For a standardized 1 MW cluster, comprising ten 100 kW sized systems, a collection of 3-4 robots specialized assigned to each 1MW cluster would have to perform around four hundred standardized swaps per year â more than one a day. This would include replacing broken or damaged parts, as well as upgrading to the server hardware itself.

Hubble has already been repaired by a crewed mission. NASA wants to do it again, Great Space expliains. Credit - Great Space YouTube Channel

Scaling that up once again to a 1 GW computer cluster, comparable to a major modern AI campus here on Earth, the number becomes staggering. There would have to be 400,000 automated replacement tasks every year. And supplying the parts to do that would require launching up to 25 metric tons of replacement cargo every day.

To put it bluntly, we donât have that kind of launch capacity yet. Nor would sending humans up help manage such a drastic workload. The paper estimates that housing and feeding a crew of 4-6 technicians to actively manage a data center constellation would require $500 million to $1.5 billion per year. Until we get to the scale of several hundred megawatts to a gigawatt-level system, that is not economically feasible.

Thatâs not to say we couldnât launch specialized crewed repair missions occasionally. But at the scales needed to make a dent in the AI infrastructure we have down here on Earth, it would be hard to keep up with the overall maintenance workload using humans. And unfortunately, the entire concept of maintenance is another area that the back-of-the-envelope calculations of the companies that want to build orbital data centers seem to ignore.

Their solution is simply to add some extra hardware to account for the inevitable damage/failure that comes with operating in space. While that might work for a little while, if the plan is to have a long-term data center presence in orbit, it's better to design for at least the possibility of continual operation rather than burning up tens of thousands of satellites in fireballs across the world every year. It remains to be seen if that message will get across to the people designing these systems, though.

S. G. Turyshev - Operations, Maintenance, and Industrial Scaling of MW-Class Orbital Data Centers

UT - The Physics Wall Facing Orbital AI Data Centers

#6406. Rep. Darren Soto survives Republican-drawn map in Florida

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, here at a hearing in July, has won a sixth term representing the 9th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.

Soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day. His margin of victory was above the 0.5 percent threshold that would trigger a recount under state law.

House Democrats have so far flipped more than 40 seats and appear on track to hold their biggest majority in the chamber in decades. Soto’s win means that no House Democratic incumbent lost to a Republican in the general election this year. And Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had hoped to pick up under the state’s new Republican-drawn map.

Democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz both won reelection from districts that shifted red, while Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, defeated Republican Marine Corps veteran Casey Askar for a redrawn open seat in South Florida.

Soto, who declared victory last week, had been seen as the most vulnerable of the targeted Florida Democrats. The new map reduced the Hispanic population of his district as the seat shifted from one that Kamala Harris would have carried in 2024 to one that Donald Trump would have taken by 18 points.

“Despite the Florida Republican legislature’s efforts to redraw me out of this district, my record of delivering for Florida showed voters that I am a reliable fighter for them in Congress,” Soto said in a Nov. 4 statement.

In a Tuesday memo detailing how House Democrats secured their historic majority, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee took aim at Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, saying their “attempts to steal seats … supremely backfired.”

While Florida Republicans were unsuccessful in flipping the four Democrat-held seats, the party held all of its House seats in the Sunshine State. Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar narrowly won reelection in the Miami-area 27th District over Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, the AP reported Tuesday. In the 7th District outside Orlando, Republican former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah defeated Democratic Navy veteran Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff who conceded Tuesday.

#6404. Scientists Uncover a Potential Root Cause of the Global Allergy Epidemic

Scientists have identified a potential biological mechanism that could explain how seemingly unrelated environmental factors contribute to the growing prevalence of allergies.

Allergies may begin with an energy crisis inside the cells that protect the body from the outside world, rather than a malfunction of the immune system. An extensive analysis led by Griffith University researchers challenges decades of conventional thinking about allergic diseases and proposes a potential biological origin for conditions ranging from eczema to food allergies.

The researchers identified abnormalities involving mitochondria, the structures responsible for producing much of the energy cells need to function. Their findings suggest that epithelial cells, which form protective barriers along the skin, gut, nose, lungs, and esophagus, may struggle to meet environmental and metabolic demands, triggering an excessive immune response.

“For 60 years, we’ve taught that allergies start with the immune system and the barrier breaks as a consequence, but our work suggests it may be the other way around,” said study lead Professor Peter Smith, a clinical immunologist from Griffith’s School of Medicine and Dentistry.

The team examined what it describes as the largest collection of multi-omic allergy data known to the researchers, drawing on 116 case-control cohorts and data from 3,776 patients. Multi-omic analysis combines different types of molecular information to identify biological patterns that might otherwise go undetected.

Scientists may have discovered the hidden cause of allergies. Credit: Professor Peter Smith, Griffith University

“Allergy diseases, which now affect up to one in three children, may start one step earlier as a power failure in the mitochondria of the epithelial cells which form the body’s barrier surfaces,” Professor Smith said.

“The barrier cell can’t meet the energy and stress demands of the modern environment so raises the alarm too easily, and the immune events we recognize as an allergy, follow.

“It could help to explain why some children have eczema, food allergies, hay fever, asthma and related conditions.”

The strongest evidence emerged in eosinophilic esophagitis, an allergic inflammatory disease affecting the esophagus. Across all 13 independent patient cohorts, researchers found reduced activity in the cellular process responsible for removing damaged mitochondria.

In patients with eczema, abnormalities affecting the skin’s protective barrier and antioxidant defenses appeared even in areas without inflammation. This finding is consistent with the possibility that cellular dysfunction precedes visible symptoms.

However, the mitochondrial signature was not universal. Researchers found only partial evidence of it in hay fever, while the pattern was absent in established asthma and nasal polyps.

The researchers propose that several environmental factors associated with allergies could converge on the same biological vulnerability: the ability of epithelial cells to generate sufficient energy and withstand stress.

Potential contributors include highly processed diets, air pollution, microplastics, detergents, declining dietary fiber intake, and antibiotic exposure early in life.

Associate Professor Nic West, a molecular immunologist from Griffith’s School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences and co-author of the study, said the wide range of factors associated with allergies has made it difficult to develop a unified explanation for their rapid increase within a single generation.

The proposed mechanism could also explain why allergic diseases frequently recur after treatment. Inflammation itself can damage epithelial cells, potentially creating a self-perpetuating cycle of barrier dysfunction and immune activation.

“The research also explains why allergies can relapse,” Associate Professor West said.

“Once inflammation is established it damages the barrier further.

“Today’s drugs act downstream, so the disease often returns when treatment stops as they do not reach the root cause.”

The researchers emphasize that their findings support a hypothesis rather than establish a definitive cause of allergies. Direct measurements of epithelial cell function before symptoms appear will be needed to determine whether mitochondrial dysfunction initiates allergic disease.

“We have spent our careers managing the smoke and for the first time we think we can see the fire, and it is not where everyone was looking,” Professor Smith said.

“This is not a cure but is something we have never had before – a logical starting point.

“The next step is to measure these cells directly in infants before the allergy develops.”

Reference: “The Origins of Allergy: An Outside-In, Bioenergetic Hypothesis” by Peter K. Smith, Nicholas P. West, Stanley Du Preez, Hugh A. Sampson, Peter W. Hellings, David Price, Liam O’Mahony, Carina Venter, Cezmi A. Akdis and Gil Yosipovitch, 29 October 2026, Allergy. DOI: 10.1111/all.70532

#6403. What 8 Cool Food People Outsource for Thanksgiving

﻿Laila Gohar, Deb Perelman, and others share their top tips

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

A few Novembers ago, I had a mild crash out over puff pastry. I was planning to meet my partner’s extended family for the first time over Thanksgiving, and volunteered to bring a holiday staple a few weeks prior (in what was one of the most helpful, albeit intimidating Excel sign-up sheets I’ve ever seen). What could be easier than apple pie? The ingredients for the recipe I found weren’t fussy, and it hardly called for fancy technical skills. Plus, I could make it ahead of time knowing that it would travel well.

Then I remembered the puff pastry. For some reason, I attached a moral imperative to the idea of making the whole pie from scratch, and spent the next two weeks poring over puff pastry recipes that felt like casual guides to wizard-tier alchemy. I loved to cook, but I simply wasn’t a big baker. (I also didn’t own a food processor, unless you counted my Magic Bullet.) My mother eventually brought me down to Earth. “Just buy it,” she told me over the phone, undoubtedly rolling her eyes. “Everyone knows it’s a pain in the butt.” Even the Barefoot Contessa herself, she reminded me, famously avoids the time-consuming task (“Nobody wants to make puff pastry!”).

Those words set me free. Once I realized that I could outsource my puff pastry, and the source of my Thanksgiving stress, I was finally able to relax and enjoy the holiday. Folks take pride in their Turkey Day dishes, as they should, but there’s nothing wrong with accepting a little help.

In the hopes of encouraging you to lighten your load, my colleague Bettina Makalintal and I asked some of the coolest people we know in the food industry what they prefer to outsource for Thanksgiving, from smoked hams to appetizers, in order to keep their holiday stress-free.

“There is a single premade item that I purchase for Thanksgiving: a smallish in-house smoked ham from The Meat Hook. It’s a sort of whatever part of the Thursday meal — I make a banging turkey, which commands most of the attention. But! The ham has become a key player during what my family calls Leftover Sandwich Weekend. Having an extra piece of protein mitigates any concerns about not having enough turkey left over. More importantly, a thin slice or two adds a salty, fatty, sweet, and smoky layer to the sandwich architecture. Much needed, very appreciated. Ham: I can’t imagine a turkey sandwich without it.” — Carla Lalli, cookbook author of books including Food is a Feeling

“I outsource pies because I don’t especially enjoy making them… or eating them!”— Laila Gohar, food-based conceptual designer, artist, and co-founder of Gohar World

“I almost always outsource appetizers and/or a cheese plate. If I’m making the big stuff (turkey, stuffing, sides, desserts… okay, I’m also a control freak with more time to cook than most), I feel absolutely overwhelmed if I am also making small things. So while I have a couple really simple apps I’ll put out if there are no volunteers, I much prefer having a friend or family member bring their favorite wedge of cheese and crackers, or [crossing fingers] bacon-wrapped dates. Here is one of my simple go-tos (it’s also in my Smitten Kitchen Every Day cookbook): herb-and-garlic baked Camembert. I’d still prefer if someone else can prep it; I don’t mind heating it up.” — Deb Perelman, cookbook author and recipe developer behind Smitten Kitchen

“We outsource lumpia from Chuck’s mom. We love having them for the holiday but don’t like frying at home when we have everything else cooking that day. She always has a couple hundred in her freezer ready and waiting to be fried for special occasions.” — Hailee Catalano and Chuck Cruz, cookbook authors and recipe developers behind @2peoplecooking

“I usually get a roast duck from Hay Hay Roasted in Chinatown, because they’ve got it down. It’s consistently delicious and not everyone eats turkey in our family.” — Camari Mick, chef and founder of Calabash

“I always outsource the pre-dinner snacks to the grocery store. I have so much respect for people who can construct elaborate cheese boards or spend the morning filling puff pastries, but that’s just not me. I like to set out a few bowls with tamari almonds, Castelvetrano olives, and — this is the most important one — Nacho Cheese Doritos. They’re the perfect mix of salty, crunchy little snacks to have with a drink before dinner is ready. The Doritos always get cleaned out first, so keep a backup bowl waiting in the kitchen.” — Casey Elsass, columnist at Cup of Jo and author of What Can I Bring?

“Last year for Friendsgiving, we collectively decided to skip the hassle of making the turkey and instead ordered Popeyes’ Cajun-Style Turkey. It’s rubbed with a blend of Louisiana-style Cajun spices and comes fully cooked, so all you have to do is thaw, heat, and serve it. It really set the tone for a very unserious dinner, which I think is what you want at a Friendsgiving. We’ll be ordering it again this year.” — Anna Archibald and Kevin Serai, content creators and recipe developers behind Cabagges.World

“We’re fairly relaxed about Thanksgiving, but if we do end up making food on that day, I usually outsource pie dough! I’m happy to buy organic frozen pie dough because usually it tastes fine and it saves me a little bit of time. I realized I prefer to spend my energy on the other parts of the meal, and I prefer not to add on to my own mental load by also making pie dough. I know it’s quick and easy; I’d just rather not! But I do make my own fillings.” — Ifrah F. Ahmed, author of Soomaaliya

#6402. Detection of Vaporized Rock Reveals the Birth of a Solar System

Astronomers have detected titanium oxide in gas form for the first time around a young, massive star. The detection offers a rare glimpse into the very earliest stages of solar system formation, before the formation of planets and asteroids.

The detection was made around a young protostar called Orion Source I, which lies some 1500 light-years from Earth. Orion Source I has not yet reached the main sequence phase of a starâs life cycle â it continues to accrete material from its surrounding molecular cloud.

Models of solar system formation have long held that certain rocky molecules, ones which are stable at high temperatures, act as the âseedsâ that make up the dust in a protoplanetary disk, and later form the basis for rocky planets like Earth and Mars. This includes elements like calcium, aluminum, and titanium. Only later do materials that vaporize easily â volatiles like water, for example â accrete to young solar system objects.

But itâs not exactly clear where these seeds form. Samples collected from our own solar system suggest that they form under high-temperature conditions. They are, as far as we can tell, the oldest solids ever formed in our solar system.

Now, for the first time, this detection of titanium oxide around Orion Source I is providing astronomers more direct evidence of vaporized rock at the dawn of a new star system.

âWe're in a unique situation with this object, Orion Source I,â said Adam Ginsburg, Associate Professor at the University of Florida and a co-author on the paper announcing the discovery. âThis object has a luminous enough star that it's evaporating the rock. We're seeing the rock evaporate from solid into gas, and so we can do the spectroscopy now and figure out what the rock is made of.â

Ginsberg and his coauthors are getting the first real glimpses at the formation environments of these rocky dust-seeding materials, which complements knowledge gathered from our own solar system.

âThe exciting thing is we're seeing the titanium oxide; we can measure how much there is, and we can start comparing our measurements to how our own solar system formed,â Ginsburg said. âIn our solar system, we can measure the ratios between different types of rocks, different elements, because we can grab those rocks and bring them into a lab.â

This isnât the first time Orion Source I has provided valuable insights into solar system formation. In 2019, salty compounds were similarly detected in the protoplanetary disk.

While the salt was found mainly in the outer disk around the star, the titanium oxide was found closer in, at the base of the starâs outflow of material: a hotter, more extreme region where the material could be vaporized. Understanding the origin of this material is an important discovery for researchers trying to piece together exactly how a new solar system comes together, and offers a glimpse into the past of our own star and rocky neighbourhood.

The detection was published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters in 2026.

Scott Johnston is a science communicator and author with a PhD in the history of science. He is the author of an academic book, âThe Clocks are Telling Lies,â that explores the history of global timekeeping, and is a senior science writer at Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics.

Wolves howl for a variety of reasons. But none of them are triggered by the sight of the moon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Wolves can bark, whimper, yip, squeak and growl, but they are most known for their iconic howl.

The eerie sound can travel vast distances and, if heard by other wolves, get them to join in with the chorus. But why do wolves howl in the first place?

Experts told Live Science that the behavior is triggered not by the sight of the moon, as is commonly believed, but by the need to maintain a complex social network.

Wolves can howl by themselves and in groups. "If a lone wolf howls, it's probably because they're separated from their pack and want to regain contact," Arik Kershenbaum, a zoologist at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science. "Members of a pack can become quite dispersed, and when they need to hunt together, or to care for pups, or when their territory is being threatened by other wolves, they need a way of returning to each other."

However, lone wolves that leave their packs may howl as well. This could be "a way of finding a new pack or mate to join," Kershenbaum said.

When a wolf pack howls together, they are sometimes advertising their territory to deter other packs. "Data shows that packs howl more in the center of their territory; they howl more when there are pups around and also when they have a carcass from a hunt," Tamás Faragó, an ethologist and bioacoustician at Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest, Hungary, told Live Science. "So group howling can have a repellent effect on neighboring packs."

However, "most chorus howling is social — that is, they howl together to build what is technically called social cohesion," Kershenbaum said, "because it makes them feel good to be safe and surrounded by their pack mates. Faragó noted that this kind of group howling gets a pack in the same mood, "and is quite common before going out on a hunt."

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Howling can trigger more howling. "When an individual wolf hears a howl, it has a very strong tendency to reply back," Faragó said. However, "if a lone wolf is accidentally wandering into the territory of its neighbors, and they hear the pack there howling, they won't respond. That would make it obvious that it's an intruder there."

A wolf's howl can be heard up to 10 miles (16 kilometers) away in open terrain, according to the Wolf Conservation Center in South Salem, New York. The combination of low- and high-frequency sounds that make up howls ensures that "even if some of the lower-frequency sounds are attenuated by vegetation, the higher-frequency components can remain intact and carry a lot of information about the individuals that made the howls," Faragó said.

Wolf pups make their first high-pitched attempts at howling between 2 to 4 weeks old.

Wolf howls differ among species and subspecies. A 2016 study of 13 species and subspecies of wolves, jackals, coyotes and dogs by Kershenbaum and his colleagues found that each has a kind of howling dialect that features different types of howls with varying regularity depending on the species or subspecies. For example, the howling repertoire of the timber wolf (Canis lycaon) is dominated by low, flat howls, while red wolves (Canis rufus) most frequently use high, looping howls.

The howling of dogs, which are descended from gray wolves (Canis lupus), can differ from wolf howling, but this depends very much on the breed. A 2023 study from Kershenbaum, Faragó and their colleagues found that more ancient dog breeds that are more closely related to wolves howl more often. In contrast, more modern dog breeds bark more often.

A question "that we all want to answer" is whether howling sounds might differ depending on their purpose, Kershenbaum said. "The problem is that most of the time when wolves howl, we don't know what they're doing at that time — they're either too far away, or it's nighttime."

Generally, "we believe that howls made in different emotional states probably sound different," Kershenbaum said. "For example, perhaps when a wolf is feeling threatened in a territorial conflict, the howl goes up and down in pitch in a different way than when the wolf is relaxed. But this is a field of active research."

A common belief is that wolves howl at the moon. "A myth, I'm afraid," Kershenbaum said. "There doesn't seem to be any correlation at all between them." He suggested that perhaps before electric lights, people were outdoors more often when there was a bright moon, "and that's when they heard the wolves."

#6400. Intermittent Fasting May Not Work the Way Scientists Thought for Liver Health

A clinical trial suggests that improving liver health may require less attention to strict fasting schedules and more emphasis on developing eating habits that people can sustain.

For people using intermittent fasting to reduce fat in the liver, finding a meal schedule that helps them lose weight may be more important than eating at specific times of the day. A new clinical trial found that people who lost at least 5% of their body weight experienced the greatest reductions in liver fat, with no clear advantage to eating earlier or later in the day.

Led by the University of Granada (UGR) and the Public University of Navarra, the multicenter study was published in JHEP Reports and involved 197 adults aged 30 to 60 with overweight or obesity. The research forms part of the doctoral dissertation of Antonio Clavero Jimeno, a predoctoral researcher at the University Joint Institute for Sport and Health (iMUDS) at UGR.

The researchers conducted a secondary analysis of a clinical trial previously published in Nature Medicine. That trial found that participants who practiced intermittent fasting lost an average of 3 to 4 kilograms (6.6 to 8.8 pounds) more than those who received only nutritional recommendations, regardless of their eating schedule. Eating earlier in the day, which in Spain often amounts to skipping dinner, also produced specific improvements in certain measures of blood sugar regulation.

To investigate whether these eating schedules offered additional benefits for liver health, the researchers compared three forms of time-restricted eating (TRE), a type of intermittent fasting that confines food consumption to specific hours of the day.

Participants were randomly assigned to four groups: standard care, early eating (approximately 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.), late eating (2 p.m. to 10 p.m.), and a self-selected eating window (12:20 p.m. to 8 p.m. on average). Over 12 weeks, all four groups received the same nutritional education program based on the Mediterranean diet and healthy lifestyle habits.

The researchers used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to measure liver fat and examined liver stiffness, liver enzymes, circulating proteins involved in liver metabolism, and other indicators of liver health.

Although liver fat decreased in all three intermittent fasting groups, none experienced statistically significant improvements beyond those achieved through standard care. The timing of meals also made no significant difference to other measures of liver health or the composition and diversity of microorganisms living in the gut.

Approximately 40 to 45% of participants practicing intermittent fasting lost at least 5% of their body weight. Reaching this threshold was associated with significantly greater reductions in liver fat, and most participants who achieved it belonged to the fasting groups. Greater reductions were also observed among people who already had hepatic steatosis, an excessive accumulation of fat in the liver, at the beginning of the study.

“The results do not suggest that intermittent fasting is ineffective, but rather that choosing an early, late, or self-selected fasting window does not appear to provide any additional benefit for liver health,” explain Manuel Dote Montero and Antonio Clavero Jimeno, the study’s first authors.

For the researchers, “the most important factor seems to be choosing a strategy that facilitates clinically significant weight loss and can be sustained over time.”

References: “Time-restricted eating, liver health, and fecal microbiota in adults with overweight or obesity: A randomized controlled trial” by Manuel Dote-Montero, Antonio Clavero-Jimeno, Adrián Cortés-Martín, Amaya Lopez-Pascual, Elisa Merchán-Ramírez, Alba Camacho-Cardenosa, Mara Concepción, Maddi Osés, Alejandro López-Vázquez, Francisco J Amaro-Gahete, Juan J Martin-Olmedo, Lucas Jurado-Fasoli, Alejandro De-la-O, Patricia V García Pérez, Julio Gálvez, Alba Rodriguez-Nogales, Federico Garcia, Carmen Mbongo Habimana, Marcos Jiménez Vázquez, Víctor Manuel Alfaro-Magallanes, Matías A Avila, Jose L Martín-Rodríguez, Rafael Cabeza, Manuel Muñoz-Torres, Idoia Labayen and Jonatan R Ruiz, 7 July 2026, JHEP Reports. Not all deals are created equal — but it’s worth scoring cult-fave ceramics, cool-LA-person food gifts, and more

We’re a far cry from the Black Friday traditions of yore. Instead of storming the gates of department stores at dawn for Salad Shooters and Cabbage Patch dolls, we now sit on our own couches to peruse the deals online — and there are lots of deals. Too many deals! But, not enough that are worthy to qualify as truly worthwhile Black Friday promotions. (Ten or 15 percent? Please.) For the most part, however, the digital age of Black Friday deal-hunting is about machete-chopping your way through the roughage of “meh” promotions.

There are exceptions: Black Friday is usually when brands who rarely run promotions release limited-time deals, and it’s the smartest time of year to buy countertop appliances and electronics. Our online-shopping experts have done the hunting for you.

Below, we’ve rounded up the best Black Friday kitchen and food deals that have already gone live, and which are actually worth your time. There are appliances you’ll use daily, dinnerware beloved by the Eater staff’s favorite restaurants, and GOATed French knives. Find the caffeinated beverage of your choice, and let’s shop.

This is the moment to invest anything you’ve ever pined over from heritage cookware brands, including the big kahuna: Le Creuset. Le Creuset’s Dutch ovens and baking dishes are going to be on escalating promotions across various retailers, so snag the colorways you love most while they’re still available.

Oft-imitated but never equaled, KitchenAid’s stand mixers last decades and look damn good on a counter, with their streamlined mid-century design and array of shades. Black Friday is the time to make the splurge, as they’re on sale across Crate & Barrel, Williams Sonoma, Amazon, and other retailers. This porcelain-white 5-quart option is a classic iteration that will look good in every kitchen, and it’s currently 30 percent off.

Renowned for their intricate craftsmanship and ergonomic, lightweight design, Laguiole knives have been made in the same eponymous French village for hundreds of years. The discounts have already started rolling out; there’s a set of six wood-handled knives on sale at Wayfair, a carving set priced down at Overstock that’ll come in handy for serving meat at future holidays, and a cream-colored set on sale at Mark and Graham that comes with the option of custom engraving.

Los Angeles-based lifestyle brand Flamingo Estate is a major fave among Eater editors, ogled for luxe items like its beloved heirloom-tomato-scented candle and Hachiya persimmon vinegar. It’s having a rare sitewide sale this week, with 20 percent off everything, including the new Big Pasta Dinner set and Affogato set with vanilla olive oil and espresso salt. Truly a one-stop-shop for fancy food gifts.

My Eater colleague Bettina Makalintal got me into Jono Pandolfi a few years ago, and the small rose-colored plates I bought with her at their holiday sale have become my favorites for plating desserts. I’m not alone: The New Jersey-based ceramic studio has an impressive roster of restaurants that use its dinnerware, including Gramercy Tavern, Lilia, and restaurants at cool hotels like the Ojai Valley Inn; that’s probably because they’re durable, come in unique colorways, and dishwasher- and microwave-safe. These gems don’t go on sale often, so add them to your cart while you can.

The best to ever do it (seriously, check out my review of the iconic Dutch coffee machine). Sometimes, I’ll warm up my marigold-colored MCM percolator and imagine that I’m Peggy from Mad Men.

This De’Longhi espresso maker is the perfect size for a smaller apartment, or anyone who has been manifesting a serious espresso machine that doesn’t cost an arm and a leg. De’Longhi is the real deal: The Italian company has been perfecting its machines since the early 1900s. I also appreciate that this more novice-friendly version comes with presets.

#6398. AI Helps Three Powerful Supercomputers Simulate The Milky Way In Extraordinary Detail

In the early days, astronomers kept sketchbooks close at hand when they looked through their telescopes. They drew what they saw and shared their drawings. Modern astronomy, with its enormous segmented lenses, gigabyte cameras, and cryogenically-cooled infrared space observatories, makes those days seem more distant than they really are. But one of the latest efforts in astronomy makes astronomy's sketch-pad days seem so far in the past, they're almost red-shifted.

In an impressive technological maneuver, astronomers have harnessed three different supercomputers together to simulate the Milky Way at a level of detail never before achieved. They used the supercomputers and AI together to simulate the Milky Way down to the level of individual stars. Up until now, the smallest level of detail in simulations, called particles, was clusters of stars with the mass of about 100 Suns. The behaviour of individual stars was averaged out in those simulations (Auriga, FIRE, etc.)

These results are in a paper titled "Architecture-Agnostic Exascale Star-by-Star Simulation of Our Galaxy," from the SC26: International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis. The lead author is Keiya Hirashima, from RIKEN in Japan.

In simulations, achieving a level of individual stars means that individually simulated particles have one solar mass. So it's like a proxy for the population of stars. But regardless of that important distinction, the new simulations are extraordinary.

"Our highest-resolution Milky Way simulation used 5.4 trillion particles, â¼ 10, 000Ã those in the state-of-the-art simulations," the authors write.

âWe expect better simulations as computational power increases, but this still requires work on improving resolutions, and for a Milky Way-sized galaxy, itâs not straightforward,â said Professor Michiko Fujii from the Department of Astronomy at the University of Tokyo. âWhen we look at smaller regions in detail, we encounter areas where the gas is denser and changes rapidly. This means the simulation needs to take much shorter steps in time, which greatly increases the amount of calculation required."

This figure from the paper shows different structures of disk galaxies at different scales, emphasizing the complexity necessary for accurate simulations. Top left and middle: NGC 4414, a disk galaxy similar to the Milky Way Galaxy, taken with the Hubble Space Telescope. Top right: NGC628, a disk galaxy with spiral arms and bubble structures taken with the JWST. Bottom left: Carina star forming region taken with the JWST. Bottom middle: Cassiopeia A supernova remnant taken with the JWST. Bottom right: turbulent innterstellar gas around Cassiopeia A taken with Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer. Image Credit: Hirashima et al. 2026. SC2026.

To achieve this fine particle resolution, simulations need ever shorter time steps, and time steps are like simulation currency; the shorter they are, the more computing resources they demand. To supply the resources for that, the researchers harnessed the power of three exascale supercomputers together: Aurora, Frontier, and JUPITER. Each one ran the same software on different hardware: Intel, NVIDIA, and AMD graphic processing units (GPUs) and central processing units (CPUs).

But linking three supercomputers was only part of the solution.

"We overcame this problem by using an AI model to predict how gas around supernova explosions evolves," said Fujii. "This allowed us to carry out the simulation more efficiently and achieve a level of detail where individual stars can be represented."

By using this model, the larger simulation was able to skip over many small timesteps. It's called PHEASANT, and it was developed by postdoctoral researcher Keiya Hirashima from RIKEN. Supernovae are complex and require their own detailed simulations with very small timesteps. By plugging PHEASANT into the larger simulation, it relieved that simulation of a lot of work.

"With trillions of particles, we resolve individual stars and model their SN feedback self-consistently within a galactic-scale simulation," the authors write. "Such a simulation reveals how individual stars, such as the Sun, contribute to the overall structure of the MW through multiple physical processes."

This image from PHEASANT shows the Milky Way's disk. Galaxies are complex structures, with different types of structures at different scales. They have thin and thick disks, bulges, halos, spiral arms, star clusters, nebulae, and individual stars and gas clouds. In this work, the researchers divided the galaxy into smaller regions that could be processed by different parts of a supercomputer. Â©2026 PHEASANT/Hirashima/Fujii CC-BY-ND

âOne of my parts was to develop an AI model that predicts how the gas surrounding a supernova explosion changes over time. If we calculate this process directly, we need time steps of around 100 years,â said Hirashima. âMy model predicts gas distribution after 100,000 years. This means that, rather than having to calculate every small step, we can use a much longer time step for the entire galaxy simulation. Making this work efficiently on different supercomputers was a challenge because each system uses different AMD, Intel, or NVIDIA CPUs and GPUs. Achieving good performance across all three systems required some specific optimizations.â

These panels are snapshots from PHEASANT. The panel on the left shows the distribution and temperature of gas across a model galaxy. The panel on the right is a close-up view, where individual stars are visible as dots. Image Credit: Â©2026 PHEASANT/Hirashima/Fujii CC-BY-ND

We can't understand the Milky Way, or galaxies in general, without a detailed understanding of how its gas and stars behave. Stars are born, drift away from their clusters, and evolve. Depending on their masses, they can remain on the main sequence for trillions of years, leave the main sequence after a few billion years and then linger as white dwarf cinders, or exhaust their fuel rapidly and explode as supernovae.

Gas is also complex. It collects in clouds where stars form, can be funnelled into the galactic center and "recycled" by supermassive black holes, or blasted away by explosions. Stars and gas are linked, and there's an extraordinary amount of detail involved.

Supernovae are among the most complicated events. In some regions, the massive young stars that eventually explode as supernova are born in the same region. When they exhaust their fuel, they explode and carve massive bubbles in the interstellar medium. That can drive gas away to form more new stars elsewhere. They can even propel gas outside of the galaxy. It's all part of the life of the Milky Way, and simulations that struggle to recreate all of the detail in supernova explosions can lead astronomers astray.

This is LHA 120-N44 (N44) in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the ESO's Very Large Telescope. It features a massive bubble excavated in the interstellar medium by exploding young stars in its center. Some of the stars are still there, and they're still expanding the bubble with their powerful winds. Simulating all of the complexity involved is an enormous challenge. Image Credit: ESO/Manu Mejias

âSomething we want to understand is how events on the scale of individual stars connect to the larger structure of the Milky Way,â said Fujii. âWith this simulation, we can investigate how individual supernovae affect the number of stars that form, the size of these giant gas bubbles and the material that flows out of the galaxy. We can also study how groups of stars form and how they may eventually develop into star clusters.â

The PHEASANT AI surrogate model plays a critical role in this work, and that's part of a broader trend in science.

"The surrogate modeling approach can also be generalized beyond astrophysical problems to other research fields," the authors write.

"AI surrogate modeling accelerates simulations and bridges wider physical scales, opening new pathways in various real-world applications, including climate modeling, space forecasting, and low-temperature plasma," the authors conclude.

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."

#6397. 2026 Was the Year Restaurants Went Full Midwest

It’s a giardinera- and tavern-style-stuffed, totally welcoming time in hospitality

At Kyle Knall’s Milwaukee restaurant Cassis, the showstopper dish is ravioli Dauphiné, a sheet of 24 tiny squares stuffed with the Wisconsin cheese Pleasant Ridge Reserve. Topped with glazed seasonal veggies, kernels of sweet corn in summer and sliced honeynut squash in late fall, it speaks to Knall’s Midwestern-meets-French approach—one of the reasons why his restaurant earned a slot on Eater’s 2026 list of the Best New Restaurants in America.

The Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, feature serious Midwest representation. The Best New Restaurants list includes Chicago’s Creepies, which also digs into that Midwest-French mashup, and Kansas City’s Akoya Omakase, which brings a distinct viewpoint to the omakase experience. Meanwhile, the pickled walleye cheeks at Rosy in Cleveland and the puffed grain toast at All Well in Chicago are among the Restaurant Dishes of the Year, and Chicago’s Bad Butter, a place best-known for its croissant take on a Chicago-style hot dog, is one of the Best New Bakeries. It even includes drinks—Culebra, a Puerto Rican spot that draws on the Latinx influences of its Chicago neighborhood, is on Punch’s Best New Bars list. Between these accolades and other national recognition, all eyes are on the Midwest right now. And that’s even before we get into the impact of the Chicago-set show The Bear, which put Italian beef on everyone’s radar, and the rise of tavern-style pizza around the country.

The Midwest has always had great restaurants, of course, but it’s undeniable that something has shifted. “People are flying into these cities rather than flying over them,” says Vinnie Cimino, the Cleveland chef who co-owns Rosy and Cordelia. “I think that word is getting out about these smaller pockets of culture and cuisine.” Some of this is attributable to diners being more willing to explore outside big coastal cities, but it’s also due to chefs returning home to the region. “Post-pandemic, a lot of folks moved out of larger cities and back home,” says Cimino. “Now they’re setting up shop and creating great things in the spaces that they grew up in.” David Posey, chef and co-owner of Creepies and Elske in Chicago, agrees, adding: “For a long time, it felt like we were playing catch-up with trends on the coasts. Now I think we’re less quick to follow trends and are more confident in having our own voice of what the Midwest is.”

One of those chefs who left New York is Knall, a Birmingham, Alabama, native who cooked at Gramercy Tavern in New York before moving to his wife’s hometown of Milwaukee in 2020. Another is Peter Hoang, who worked at his father’s Kansas City, Missouri, sushi restaurant before gaining experience in Chicago and New York restaurants. When he returned to open Akoya Omakase, he crafted menus with the audience in mind, with two omakases, priced more affordably than many at $85 and $165, as well as an à la carte menu. “My sushi is honed by Japanese techniques and sourcing,” he says. “But I interpret what I think is best for the fish, whether that’s highlighting the textures and flavors through different garnishes or using aging or salting techniques.”

It’s not simply that these are good restaurants located in the Midwest—these restaurants are deeply Midwestern in ethos. In Chicago, David and Anna Posey, who run the Michelin-starred Elske, wanted to open a French bistro for their second venture. But as they developed Creepies with chef de cuisine Tayler Ploshehanski, David Posey says they began expanding its focus: “We started taking flavors and adapting them to things that we’re a little more familiar with.” This means dishes that draw on the traditions of Michigan, Wisconsin, and Illinois—think tarte flambée on a tavern-style pizza crust and mussels with giardiniera. And it’s not just the food at Creepies that reflects the Midwest: “We told our designer that our inspiration board was a Midwest basement with wood paneling and low ceilings meets a bistro in the French countryside.”

At Cordelia, Cimino leans into the traditional cuisine of Northeast Ohio, with offerings like raw-beef cannibal sandwiches and kielbasa with cabbage salad. “It’s the familiar flavors that we grew up eating, rethought into this more modern light,” he says. Meanwhile, Rosy “is a deeper dive into the culture of our region” and features dishes like Balkan cevapi and Italian cotechino cooked over live fire. The approach is drawing a wide range of Cleveland diners, from 20-somethings there for the cool, candlelit vibe to grandparents there to taste the food they grew up with. “I think that’s what the Midwest is,” Cimino says. “Being able to be that transgenerational space everybody feels welcome in.”

That welcoming community sensibility is a key component of Midwestern restaurants. Knall counts several farmers and shoppers at the West Allis Farmers Market, where he sources for Cassis, as some of his regulars. “To me, it shows that’s really what Midwest food is: supporting those communities,” he says.

Perhaps more than anything, it’s hospitality that sets these spots apart. “Hospitality is our biggest focus between both restaurants and maybe even more of a focus than the food,” Knall says. “To me, the way that our team makes you feel in the restaurants is such a Midwest thing.” And at Cordelia, where the slogan is “Midwest Nice,” Cimino says: “It’s welcoming you into our proverbial home.”

#6396. Scientists Discover 130-Year-Old Fish Still Swimming in an American River

Some fish swimming in Montana’s Upper Missouri River today may have hatched before the 20th century began. Researchers have confirmed that blue suckers can live up to 130 years, more than three times their previously estimated lifespan of roughly 40 years. The discovery places the species among the longest-lived vertebrates in North America.

The findings, published in Communications Biology, come from a study co-led by Alec Lackmann of the University of Minnesota Duluth, Luke Holmquist of Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks, and Allen Andrews of the University of Hawai’i at Mānoa. By examining microscopic structures inside the fishes’ heads and using a chemical signature left by nuclear weapons testing, the scientists uncovered evidence of extraordinary longevity and a population increasingly dominated by old individuals.

The blue sucker (Cycleptus elongatus) is native to 23 U.S. states but is classified as imperiled in 22 of them. For decades, researchers monitoring the Upper Missouri River have observed increasingly large fish and remarkably few juveniles. The pattern suggests that young blue suckers have struggled to survive and join the adult population.

“For decades, there has been conservation concern for the species across much of its range,” the researchers wrote. “Nonetheless, no validated age-based life history information exists for the species, which is a major knowledge gap.”

To investigate, the team collected and examined nearly 50 blue suckers between 2023 and 2026. More than 60 percent were older than 90 years, and some had survived for approximately 130 years. Their age distribution suggests that successful recruitment of new generations has become less frequent since major dams were installed in the mid-1900s. Habitat fragmentation associated with those dams is a possible contributor, although the study does not establish it as the cause.

The researchers determined the fishes’ ages by examining otoliths, tiny structures commonly called earstones that occur in approximately 97 percent of fish species. These structures grow throughout a fish’s life, accumulating annual layers that scientists can count under a microscope, much like the growth rings of a tree.

Blue suckers presented a technical challenge because their otoliths are exceptionally small. “Blue suckers have extremely small otoliths, smaller than the buffalofishes, but we figured out how to work with them,” Lackmann said.

As the researchers examined the growth layers, they encountered ages that far exceeded established expectations. In fish previously thought to live around four decades, “we were seeing the population had ages up to 130 years old,” Lackmann said. “When age estimates are that much older than previously thought, an additional line of evidence is needed to rigorously test their validity.”

To independently verify the ages, the team turned to bomb radiocarbon dating, a technique that uses the atmospheric changes caused by nuclear weapons testing during the Cold War. Those tests produced a distinctive increase in radioactive carbon-14 that became incorporated into living organisms, including the tissues of fish.

“Thermonuclear bombs that were tested in the mid to late 1950s and early 1960s more than doubled the amount of radiocarbon in the atmosphere,” said Lackmann.

“This left a time-specific marker in organisms that lived through the bomb pulse. And if you’re able to quantify growth bands in an individual (for example, in trees, otoliths of bony fish, etc.) that is estimated to have lived through the bomb pulse, you can actually test to determine if the ages you are quantifying are accurate. Bomb radiocarbon dating is one of the best ways to age-validate long-lived organisms. So that’s where we have multiple lines of evidence here, otoliths providing the age estimates, and bomb radiocarbon confirming and validating the otolith ages and extreme longevity of the blue sucker.”

By comparing the carbon-14 signatures in the otoliths with the known timing of the atmospheric radiocarbon increase, the researchers validated the ages estimated from the growth layers. This independent evidence confirmed that blue suckers can survive for more than a century.

The blue sucker is now the fourth member of the sucker fish family (Catostomidae) found to reach 100 years or older, joining the bigmouth buffalo, smallmouth buffalo, and black buffalo. All four species have had their exceptional longevity documented since 2019, partly through advances in fish aging techniques.

Blue suckers also challenge expectations about how river environments shape animal lifespans. Unlike fish inhabiting relatively calm lakes, they spend their lives in fast-flowing rivers, where maintaining position and navigating currents can require considerable energy. Such environments have often been associated with faster life histories, making the species’ extreme longevity particularly unexpected.

The oldest fish examined had already been alive for decades when many of the dams now shaping the Missouri River system were constructed. Their survival across more than a century of environmental change contrasts with the apparent scarcity of younger generations, raising conservation concerns about whether aging adults are being replaced.

“To put a timeline on some of those older fish: the oldest one hatched around two years after Montana became a state, around the dawn of the automobile, like 20 years before the Titanic sank – it’s just wild,” said Holmquist.

“We start putting it in the context of what the landscape looked like when these fish hatched, and all the changes that have happened since—and they just keep swimming along in the river.”

Reference: “Bomb-radiocarbon validated otoliths reveal 130-year lifespans and declining recruitment for blue sucker Cycleptus elongatus of the Upper Missouri River, Montana, USA” by Alec R. Lackmann, Allen H. Andrews, Luke M. Holmquist, Negar Haghipour, Grant Grisak, Molly A. H. Webb, Mark E. Clark and Zachary R. Shattuck, 18 November 2026, Communications Biology. DOI: 10.1038/s42003-026-11219-3

Funding for this project was provided by Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks and NorthWestern Energy. The study was also coauthored by Negar Haghipour (ETH Zürich), Grant Grisak (NorthWestern Energy), Molly Webb (USFWS), Mark Clark (UMD – Biology), and Zach Shattuck (MTFWP).
