#6383. Three Ancient Cosmic Collisions May Explain Why the Moon Has Two Faces

Scientists have narrowed down when three massive collisions reshaped the Moon, bringing them closer to understanding why its Earth-facing side looks so different from its far side.

Billions of years ago, a collision powerful enough to melt enormous quantities of lunar rock created the Moon’s largest impact basin. Subsequent collisions broke apart and scattered some of that ancient material across the surface, leaving behind a geological record that scientists are now piecing together.

Located on the Moon’s far side, the South Pole-Aitken (SPA) basin is one of the oldest and largest impact structures in the solar system. Understanding its history could help explain why the Moon’s near and far sides are so different, what lies beneath its surface, and when major collisions occurred during its early evolution.

An international research team led by Professor Guochun Zhao, Mok Sau-King, a professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences (DEPS) at the University of Hong Kong (HKU), and Dr. Yuqi Qian, the study’s first author, has identified two types of magnesium-rich rocks with remarkably different origins. Published in Science Advances, the research also establishes a clearer timeline of the major impacts that shaped the region.

For decades, the basin remained largely unexplored. That changed in 2019, when Chang’e-4 completed the first successful landing on the Moon’s far side, followed in 2024 by Chang’e-6, which brought the first rock samples from this largely unexplored region back to Earth.

Using Chang’e-6 samples allocated to HKU DEPS and surface measurements from both missions, the researchers obtained the first direct geological evidence from the two landing sites for reconstructing the basin’s impact history. Satellite observations and numerical simulations helped them trace the origins of rocks across the wider basin.

One group of rocks, known as moderately magnesium-rich norites, formed in the aftermath of the original SPA collision. The impact generated a thick sheet of molten rock that gradually cooled, with different minerals crystallizing at different stages. Later collisions exposed these ancient rocks at the central peaks of large craters. Some were eventually blasted toward the Chang’e-4 landing site in Von Kármán crater by the impact that formed Finsen crater.

The second group contained considerably more magnesium and likely formed through a separate process called magnesium-suite magmatism, a type of magma activity associated with the original SPA impact. These rocks were exposed along the western ring of mountain peaks within the Apollo basin before the Chaffee S impact scattered some of them toward the Chang’e-6 landing site.

Earlier research by the HKU-led team had already uncovered evidence of prolonged volcanic activity and previously unrecognized magma activity in the region. Those studies also suggested that underground accumulations of titanium-rich minerals, known as ilmenite-bearing cumulates, helped account for the contrasting volcanic histories of the Moon’s two sides.

The latest findings suggest that the South Pole-Aitken basin formed approximately 4.34 billion years ago. Another major collision created the Apollo basin around 4.2 billion years ago, followed by the formation of the Orientale basin approximately 3.87 billion years ago. Together, these three events reveal how successive collisions reshaped the Moon’s largest impact basin over hundreds of millions of years.

Reference: “Postimpact evolution of the South Pole–Aitken basin revealed by Chang’e-4 and Chang’e-6” by Yuqi Qian, Wenlei Song, James Head, Mingyu Tian, Zhuang Guo, Harald Hiesinger, Carolyn H. van der Bogert, Le Zhang, Jingyou Chen, Wanfeng Zhang, Ziqing Li, Lingzhi Sun, Xiangsong Wang, Wei-Ran Li, Jiacheng Liu, Nicolas Dauphas, Yi-Gang Xu and Guochun Zhao, 18 November 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh9798

#6382. Experimental Drug Shrinks Tumors in Two of the Hardest-To-Treat Cancers

A single experimental drug designed to block signals from several cancer-driving mutations has shown encouraging early results, raising the possibility of treating multiple hard-to-treat cancers.

When pancreatic or lung cancer continues to grow despite several treatments, doctors can find themselves with few remaining options. In some patients, the difficulty lies in genetic mutations that keep cancer cells growing and have historically been difficult to target with drugs. An experimental cancer drug called ERAS-0015 has shown promising results in an early clinical trial, shrinking tumors in patients who had already undergone other forms of treatment.

The drug targets RAS, a family of genes that provide instructions for making proteins involved in controlling cell growth and division. In healthy cells, RAS proteins act like molecular switches, turning on when cells receive signals to grow and turning off when those signals are no longer needed. Certain genetic mutations can leave these switches stuck in the “on” position, continuously instructing cells to grow and helping sustain cancer.

For years, scientists struggled to develop drugs capable of interfering with these faulty proteins. ERAS-0015 takes an approach known as a pan-RAS molecular glue. It works by bringing proteins together at the molecular level and is designed to bind to RAS while the switch is active, blocking growth signals associated with several different cancer-driving RAS mutations.

“The overall goal of precision oncology is to match a patient’s mutation, or the ‘Achilles Heel’ of a specific individual’s cancer, to a drug that directly targets that mutation. This is what we are attempting to do by studying the effectiveness of ERAS-0015 in patients with RAS alterations,” said Dr. Judy Wang, a medical oncologist at Florida Cancer Specialists and Research Institute in Sarasota, Florida.

Wang presented findings from 148 patients participating in the phase I AURORAS-1 clinical trial on November 19, 2026, at the 38th EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona, Spain.

The trial began in June 2025 and is evaluating ERAS-0015 both alone and in combination with other anticancer therapies. Participants include people with pancreatic cancer, colorectal (bowel) cancer, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that has spread beyond the original tumor site, and other solid tumors driven by RAS mutations. The results presented at the symposium included 83 patients with pancreatic cancer and 37 with NSCLC. The trial is continuing to enroll patients.

“AURORAS-1 has enrolled patients that have tried a number of other treatments for their cancer. In this context, ERAS-0015 treatment caused a 44% response rate in patients with RAS-mutant pancreatic cancer and a 60% response rate in patients with RAS-mutant lung cancer. A ‘response’ means the patients experienced considerable tumor shrinkage, and these response rates are important as they show clinically meaningful activity from ERAS-0015 treatment in patient groups that have few if any therapeutic options to address their cancer. In addition to this, ERAS-0015 was well tolerated with few severe side effects,” Wang told the symposium.

These response rates came from relatively small groups of patients receiving a 32 mg dose of the drug. Tumors shrank in 11 of 25 patients with pancreatic cancer who had previously received chemotherapy and in three of five patients with lung cancer who had previously been treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors, drugs that help the immune system recognize and attack cancer, or platinum-based chemotherapy.

Researchers gradually increased doses of ERAS-0015 from 2 mg to 40 mg to evaluate how well patients tolerated the drug. After a median follow-up of just over four months, there was no indication that the maximum tolerated dose had been reached.

At doses of 16 to 32 mg, the most common side effects, affecting at least 10% of patients, were rash, diarrhea, nausea, and inflammation of the lining of the mouth. Twelve patients (9.8%) experienced severe treatment-related side effects, classified as grade 3 or higher. No dose-limiting side effects were reported.

“We are encouraged by the preliminary clinical activity and tolerability of ERAS-0015 in patients that have tried a number of other treatments for RAS-driven lung and pancreatic cancer,” said Wang.

“Our goal is to give clinicians new, better options for treating their patients with RAS-driven cancers. Early results suggest ERAS-0015 has the potential to be one of these options.”

Phase I clinical trials involve relatively small numbers of patients and are primarily designed to evaluate safety and determine appropriate doses. Although the tumor shrinkage observed in this trial provides an early indication of the drug’s potential, larger phase II and phase III clinical trials will be necessary to confirm its safety and effectiveness.

“If these early results are confirmed, ERAS-0015 could offer patients with RAS-driven cancers a new option. Clinical development of ERAS-0015 would be impossible without the patients, caregivers, investigators and participating trial centers that put their trust in us to take part in our study. We are deeply grateful for their contribution to AURORAS-1,” Wang concluded.

Professor Elena Garralda, chair of the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium and co-director of the Vall d’Hebron Institute of Oncology’s clinical research program, was not involved in the study. She commented: “This is the first presentation of these preliminary results from the AURORAS-1 clinical trial and they have been eagerly awaited. They show that the RAS inhibitor, ERAS-0015, has encouraging anti-tumor activity in cancers that are hard to treat successfully and for which there are few treatment options available. We look forward to further results from larger clinical trials, which are investigating whether ERAS-0015 can help a broader group of patients.

“This is one of several studies being presented at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium that are beginning to show it is possible to design drugs that target cancers driven by RAS mutations, which was not thought possible until recently.”

#6380. Benchmade Just Knocked 20% Off Three of Its Most Popular Knives for Black Friday

Yes, that includes the Osborne and the Bugout.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

We’re constantly testing and writing about pocket knives here at Popular Mechanics, and Benchmade is a brand that always tops our list of favorites. Its folders, automatics, flippers, and fixed blades are beautifully designed using all high-quality materials, and all are U.S.-made in its Oregon headquarters. But there’s no denying they’re pricey, costing upward of $200, and they rarely go on sale for much of a discount.

But right now, ahead of Black Friday, Benchmade is knocking 20 percent off three of its most popular knives on Amazon—the Osborne, the Bugout, and the Bailout—for a savings of roughly $70 each.

When the Osborne debuted in 2000, it was Benchmade’s first blade to sport the Axis lock, which been replicated in some form by nearly every major knife manufacturer since its patent expired in 2019. It’s designed for ambidextrous operation and fast, one-handed deployment, plus it keeps your fingers clear of the blade while you open and close the knife.

This seasonal version uses CPM-S90V stainless super steel, which offers great edge retention and reliable toughness for everyday tasks like opening boxes. It’s coated with a protective distressed finish to make the reverse tanto-style blade look rustic and has a rich-looking dark-green aluminum handle, with copper accents. It feels good in hand—a durable yet lightweight EDC knife.

The Bugout is the knife our resident expert Justin Park grabs first for backpacking, camping and hunting and says it’s “arguably the defining pocket knife of the explosion of modern EDC blades.” It’s strong, but ultra lightweight and hardly registers in your pocket or pack.

Like the Osborne above, the Bugout uses S90V stainless super steel, featuring a shorter drop-point blade, copper accents, and handle that combines the same dark-green aluminum with a grippy and rugged-looking canvas micarta.

The Bailout is lightweight and tough. It has a longer drop-point tanto-style S90V stainless steel blade covered in the same stonewashed protective finish as the Bugout and Osborne, along with the same dark-green aluminum handle and copper accents. While it’s another great choice for EDC, the Bailout is outfitted with tactical-style elements, like the lanyard slot at the rear and the deep-carry clip.

Rachel is the Deputy Editor of Reviews for Hearst's Enthusiast and Wellness Group where she supports Popular Mechanics, Runner's World, and Best Products. Her background is in service journalism and earlier in her career she worked as a daily newspaper reporter and book editor. She spent more than a decade as a staff editor and writer at TripAdvisor and Penguin Random House and her byline has appeared in Time Out New York, the New York Daily News, and New York Magazine. Outside of work, Rachel can be found planning her next trip, visiting museums and galleries, and walking her wirehaired dachshund in Central Park.

#6379. An Overlooked Metabolic Byproduct Could Help Repair a Damaged Heart

A substance often treated as waste may be vital to the heart during a crisis, offering a potential target for treating heart failure and heart attacks.

The heart has to keep beating whether the body has plenty of energy available or is running low. Maintaining that constant supply of energy is a complicated process, and when it breaks down, it can contribute to serious cardiovascular conditions such as heart failure. Researchers at University of Utah Health have now uncovered an unusual feature of heart muscle cells that helps them stay fueled during periods of stress and could point toward new ways to treat a damaged heart.

Scientists previously knew that the heart could draw energy from two carbohydrate sources at once: glucose, a sugar, and lactate, a substance produced when cells break down glucose. In most human tissues, increasing the use of one fuel makes it harder to use the other. Heart muscle somehow avoids this competition.

In a study published in Nature, researchers discovered that heart muscle cells process these fuels in separate parts of the cell. Glucose is broken down in the cytosol, the fluid that surrounds structures inside the cell, while lactate is used inside mitochondria, which produce much of the cell’s usable energy. Keeping these processes separate allows the heart to draw energy from both sources simultaneously.

The system depends on a molecule called MCT1, which transports lactate into the mitochondria. The researchers found that genetic mutations affecting MCT1 prevented lactate from entering the mitochondria and disrupted the heart’s energy balance. Although the heart could largely function without this pathway under everyday conditions, losing it when the heart was under stress led to heart failure.

“This appears to be a critical backup system for heart function,” says Gregory Ducker, PhD, assistant professor of biochemistry at University of Utah Health and senior author of the study. “In an emergency, we would really, really rely on this.”

The discovery identifies a previously unrecognized role for lactate in sustaining injured heart muscle and gives researchers a potential target for developing treatments that restore its energy supply.

“Our findings help point to new areas in which we could target the heart muscle to benefit and repair itself by allowing it to use lactate better,” Ducker says. “That’s the long-term goal: to help the heart muscle heal.”

Whether enhancing this energy pathway can improve heart function in patients remains to be established, though the researchers see potential applications beyond heart failure.

“Rather than simply releasing lactate into the bloodstream as a waste product, we may be able to enhance the heart’s ability to use it as a valuable source of energy,” says Stavros Drakos, MD, PhD, professor of medicine at University of Utah Health and co-senior author of the study. “By optimizing this process, we could potentially improve heart muscle function in patients suffering from heart failure or heart attacks.”

Reference: “MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism” by Ahmad A. Cluntun, Joseph R. Visker, Jesse N. Velasco-Silva, James Carrington, Luis Cedeño-Rosario, Giulia C. Napoli, Ji Eon Kim, Thirupura S. Shankar, Marisa J. Brothwell, Rana Hamouche, Álvaro J. Narbona-Pérez, Jing Ling, Ashish G. Toshniwal, Hayden K. Low, Corey N. Cunningham, David R. Eberhardt, Jing Li, Claire E. Stanley, Queren A. Alcantara, Tarun Yadav, Ryan L. Maves, Wojciech I. Swiatek, Nicholas A. Offei, Bhavya Blaze, Sumangala P. Shetty, Dipayan Chaudhuri, Tingting Hong, Jeffery D. Rothstein, Deborah M. Muoio, Joao A. Paulo, Steven P. Gygi, Eleni Tseliou, Sutip Navankasattusas, James E. Cox, Katsuhiko Funai, Stavros G. All the must-see supermoons, meteor showers, star clusters, constellations and deep sky objects this winter — and the gear you need to see them.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Winter is an incredible time for stargazing. With the long hours of darkness and an impressive variety of celestial objects on display, it's easy to fall in love with the night sky during the winter. Whether you have binoculars, a telescope, a smart telescope or are just observing with your eyes, there's something for everyone to enjoy over the coming months.

We've listed all the best sights to see this winter, including the supermoons, star clusters, galaxies and deep-sky nebulae that are best placed in the sky in December, January and February. We see the return of Orion and the Pleiades, with Jupiter and Saturn also making their way back into the night sky, while December also has one of the best and brightest meteor showers of the entire year — the Geminids.

This is by no means an exhaustive list of everything you can see — we'd be here until July — but just a collection of some of our favorite winter sights. Some, like the supermoons and planets, are specific to 2026/2027 timings, but the constellations and deep sky objects we see over the winter are something stargazers look forward to all year. Something to get us through the cold, dreary weather, and a reassuring sign that we made it through another year.

A composite photo of a full supermoon rising into the sky.

This winter is host to three consecutive supermoons (in addition to the full Beaver Supermoon on Nov. 24, making four in a row). The first, and the most festive, is the Christmas Eve supermoon, peaking on December 24, 2026, at 01:28 UTC (which works out as late evening on the 23rd in North America). This last moon of the year is traditionally called the Cold Moon, and this supermoon will look up to 14% larger and 30% brighter than a normal full moon.

The first full moon of 2027, known as the Wolf Moon, peaks on January 22, 2027 at 12:17 UTC. Finally, the super Snow Moon peaks on February 20, 2027 at 23:24 UTC, coinciding with a penumbral lunar eclipse. This is when the sun, moon and Earth line up loosely during a full moon, causing the moon to pass through the Earth's faint outer shadow — the penumbra. During this type of eclipse, the moon only dims slightly, so it won't be nearly as dramatic as a blood moon eclipse.

A photo of an annular, or "ring of fire", solar eclipse.

Observers in South America and Africa will witness an annular solar eclipse on February 6, 2027, peaking at around 16:00 UTC. It will appear as a "ring of fire" in the sky, as an annular solar eclipse happens when the moon passes between Earth and the sun when the moon is near or at its farthest from Earth, known as apogee. Unlike a total solar eclipse, the sun isn't totally blocked, and the sky doesn't turn dark.

A photo of a bright planet glowing in the evening sky.

Since Saturn made its return to the evening sky in the fall, it rises earlier and earlier over the winter months, making this a great time to observe Saturn at a reasonable hour. There are still a few years before we will see the rings at full tilt again, but in 2026/2027 we can start to see more details in the rings after the planet appeared edge-on last year.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

To get a good glimpse of Saturn this winter, you'll need a telescope with at least 4 or 5 inches of aperture and a good eyepiece that gives you at least 100x magnification. Smart telescopes and binoculars don't have the reach, so this is a job for an observational telescope. But that's all right; the hill we'll die on is that there's nothing that'll take your breath away quite like seeing Saturn's rings with your own eyes.

Jupiter will reach opposition on the night of February 10-11, 2027, when it will be at its brightest and closest to Earth, making it appear its largest in the sky. This is the perfect time to observe it with your telescope to see the bands and the Great Red Spot, as well as its four Galilean moons. You'll be able to see the moons with a pair of big astronomy binoculars (we can see them with our 15x70’s), but you'll need a telescope to make out any of the finer details on the planet itself.

After almost a year of absence, Mars made its return to the evening sky in November (albeit quite late in the evening) and will reach opposition on February 19, 2027. Despite being one of our closest neighboring planets, Mars is notoriously difficult to get any meaningful observations with via a telescope, so its opposition is the best chance you'll have.

You'd be forgiven for thinking that because Mars is technically closer to Earth than Jupiter, Saturn and deep-sky objects like the Andromeda Galaxy or the Orion Nebula, viewing it through a telescope would be a breeze, but that's not the case. Mars is very small, with low-contrast features, and only comes observably close to Earth for a few months at a time around every 26-27 months, so it demands quite a lot from a telescope. Even with larger telescopes, it'll only show up as a fuzzy orange dot most of the time.

If you want to try viewing Mars with a telescope this opposition, you'll need 4-6 inches of aperture minimum, depending on what kind of telescope you have. However, for Mars, it's arguably more important to have good seeing (unfortunate with the nearly full moon on this day), excellent quality optics, a stable (preferably motorized) mount, a good focuser and an eyepiece with good eye relief that gives 100x magnification or more to observe any of the planet's finer details.

Alternatively, if you're more of a beginner and are just starting your stargazing hobby, you can head outside with just your eyes and go "Hey look, there's Mars. Cool!" and be done with it.

The Geminids meteor shower is active from December 4-20, peaking on the night of December 13-14, 2026. The waxing crescent moon sets early, leaving dark skies after around 9 pm for prime meteor viewing, and this is one of the few meteor showers that very kindly peaks before midnight.

The Geminids are one of the strongest meteor showers of the year, and this year’s show is expected to have around 120 to 150 meteors per hour under clear, dark skies — making it an exciting opportunity for astrophotography.

Unlike most meteor showers, which come from icy comets, the Geminids originate from a rocky asteroid called 3200 Phaethon. The debris from this asteroid is much denser than the dust from comets, making it able to survive deeper into the atmosphere before burning up. This results in brighter, stronger and more colorful fireballs than the other meteor showers.

If the Geminids left you hooked on meteor showers, you'll only have a few weeks to wait until the Ursids peak on December 22-23, 2026.

However, there are a couple of hurdles here. First, the activity rate is usually quite low — between 5 and 10 meteors per hour. Second, the nearly full moon will hinder visibility and limit sightings to only the brightest meteors. However, as they originate from Ursa Minor, which is circumpolar, the peak viewing time of 21:00-22:00 UTC is much friendlier than the showers that peak in the middle of the night, so it won't require an unreasonable amount of commitment if you do want to catch them.

The first meteor shower of 2027, the Quadrantids, is active between December 28, 2026 and January 28, 2027, peaking on the night of January 3-4, 2027. The thin waning crescent moon won't interfere with viewing conditions, and we could see up to 100-120 meteors per hour. The best time to view will be from midnight through to the pre-dawn hours, when the radiant point, Bootes, is highest in the sky.

Canis Major (the "Greater Dog") is visible over the winter months through until spring, and is easily recognisable by Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky. It's one of the closest stars to our solar system, sitting 8.6 light-years away, and due to its distance and apparent magnitude, its twinkling and flashes of color are particularly noticeable. This is known as scintillation, where turbulence in Earth's atmosphere bends starlight as it passes through different layers of air. It's especially noticeable when Sirius is low in the sky, as the light has more atmosphere to pass through.

You don't need any specialist gear to spot Sirius — it's easily visible with the naked eye. However, if you do have a pair of binoculars, you can even try to spot it in the daytime at certain times of the year.

Look above Canis Major, and you'll find Canis Minor — the "Little Dog". It primarily consists of two bright stars: Procyon and Gomeisa, the former making up a key part of the Winter Triangle and Winter Hexagon. Canis Minor is a fairly faint constellation, but a pair of binoculars will give you a better view.

Canis Minor and Canis Major are most famously known as the loyal hunting dogs of Orion, who spent seven years pursuing the Pleiades sisters to no avail. He should have just led with the fact that he had two dogs.

Speaking of Orion, one of the most recognizable sights in the night sky is Orion's belt, consisting of three bright stars in a straight line: Alnitak, Alnilam and Mintaka. Because of its prominence in the winter sky, Orion's belt has served as a universal celestial marker for navigation, timekeeping and mythologies across human history. The entire Orion constellation is a favorite among stargazers because there's so much to see, both with the naked eye and through binoculars or a telescope.

Another prominent feature of the Orion constellation is Betelgeuse. This red supergiant is easily visible to the naked eye, and astronomers expect it to explode as a supernova within the next 100,000 years. When that eventually happens, it will become visible in broad daylight and shine as brightly as the full moon for a few months. Betelgeuse, Sirius (Canis Major) and Procyon (Canis Minor) make up the Winter Triangle.

There's also Rigel, the brightest star in the constellation, which marks the hunter's foot, and Orion's Sword, a hanging line of stars just below the belt, which contains the Orion Nebula (more on that later).

Although Taurus returned to the evening sky in the fall, winter offers the best viewing time because it sits higher earlier in the evening. The brightest star in the constellation, Aldebaran, is easily recognizable as an orange-red star that marks the bull's eye.

With a pair of binoculars, you'll be able to see two beautiful star clusters — the Pleiades (M45) and the Hyades. The former is a bright open star cluster consisting of seven stars (also known as the Seven Sisters) that you can just about see with the naked eye under very dark skies, and the latter is a V-shaped open cluster that forms the face and head of the bull.

The Pleiades is an ideal first target if you're thinking of buying an entry-level smart telescope, and it's also easy to pick out in wide-field iPhone photos of the night sky.

Auriga is a pentagon-shaped constellation high in the sky between Taurus and Gemini, and is home to a few star clusters to observe this winter.

M36, the Pinwheel Cluster, contains around 60 to 100 stars and is located north of the star El Nath in Auriga. M38, known as the Starfish Cluster, contains over 100 stars, with its brightest forming an X shape, giving it a starfish-like appearance. Finally, M37, known as the Salt and Pepper Cluster, is the brightest and richest cluster in the constellation and contains over 500 stars.

Not only is Gemini the radiant point of the Geminids meteor shower, but its two most prominent stars, Pollux and Castor, are a very recognizable winter target in the night sky. Pollux is an orange giant star and the constellation's brightest point, while Castor appears blue. Although Castor looks like one star to the naked eye, it's actually a complex multiple star system, consisting of three distinct binary pairs: Castor A, Castor B and Castor C. With a small telescope, you can split Castor into its two main pairs, Castor Aa and Castor Ba.

Gemini also contains M35, a large open cluster also known as the Shoe Buckle Cluster, which you can easily view with binoculars.

It’s not an official constellation, but the Winter Hexagon (also known as the Winter Circle) is a recognizable pattern of prominent stars in the winter sky. It consists of Rigel (Orion), Aldebaran (Taurus), Capella (Auriga), Pollux (Gemini), Procyon (Canis Minor) and Sirius (Canis Major).

Once you spot all of the stars that make up the Winter Hexagon, it provides an easy way to navigate your way around the night sky with your binoculars or telescope.

Probably everyone's favorite nebula, largely because it's very easy to spot. It's located in Orion's sword, just below Orion's belt, and when conditions are dark enough, you can even see it with the naked eye and identify it in smartphone photos. Binoculars reveal it as a faint smudge, while telescopes give you a better view of the bright, glowing gas. It's also a wonderful target for smart telescopes with a wide field of view.

While you're there, you can find the Running Man Nebula, a bright reflection nebula complex located just north of the Orion Nebula — and it can be captured in the same frame if you're photographing it. If nebulas are your thing, Orion is absolutely packed with them, including the Casper the Friendly Ghost Nebula (M78), the Monkey Head Nebula (NGC 2174) and the Witch Head Nebula (IC 2118), although many of Orion's nebulas are quite faint and tricky to capture, requiring long integration times.

A photo of the Horsehead and Flame Nebulas

The Horsehead and Flame Nebula in Orion is another popular target for smart telescopes, as it takes up a big portion of the frame and doesn't need a super-long integration time to get a decent, web-ready image (although we'd always recommend shooting for as long as you can).

The Flame and Horsehead are technically two separate entities, but are often paired together due to their close apparent proximity, often fitting inside the same frame. The Flame Nebula is a bright, vibrant emission nebula that gets its name from its fiery network of dark, dense dust lanes. The Horsehead Nebula, on the other hand, is a dark nebula. It's composed of a dense cloud of molecular dust and gas that blocks the light from the emission nebula and stars around it. As the name suggests, this dark nebula takes on the form of a horse's head and neck.

The Rosette Nebula is a vast, star-forming region in the constellation of Monoceros and is a fantastic astrophotography target. Its large, flower-like appearance comes from stellar winds and radiation from the central cluster of young stars. The best time to view and photograph the Rosette Nebula is from January, when Monoceros climbs higher and higher in the evening sky.

The California Nebula lives in the constellation Perseus and gets its name from its resemblance to the U.S. state. This famous emission nebula is made up of ionized gas from the nearby Xi Persei, giving it its vibrant red and pink appearance. It has an apparent size of approximately 2.5 degrees, making it a great target for astrophotography and smart telescopes, as it appears quite large in the frame. Peak visibility of the California Nebula is from now until February.

12,000 light-years away, in the constellation Auriga, you'll find the Tadpole Nebula — a beautiful emission nebula and active stellar nursery. It spans 100 light-years across and makes for a stunning smart telescope target. It gets its name from the distinct, prominent gas and dust pillars that resemble cosmic tadpoles swimming through space — only these tadpoles are around 10 light-years long.

If you're using a smart telescope or astrophotography camera, you'll typically need an integration time of 2-3 hours to bring out more structure in the nebulosity, although longer sessions will yield better results.

Also in Auriga is the Flaming Star Nebula, although this nebula is much closer to Earth — around 1,500 light-years away — and spans about 5 light-years across. Despite being "smaller" than other targets, it appears quite big in the frame of a smart telescope due to its distance from Earth. It's best seen throughout late autumn and winter when Auriga is climbing high in the sky.

The Flaming Star Nebula is an emission and reflection nebula, with each type of nebulosity responding to different filters. In this instance, capturing two sets of data to stack in astrophotography software can help reveal more detail and colors. Broadband filter exposures capture the full range of visible light, including the blue light reflected by dust, as well as natural star colors. Narrowband or dual-band filters isolate specific emission wavelengths, such as hydrogen-alpha (Ha) and oxygen-III (OIII). By using these filters for separate sessions, your final image will show the red glow from the emission nebula and the blue tones from the reflective dust.

Kimberley Lane, E-commerce writer for Live Science, has tested a wide range of optical equipment, reviewing camera gear from Sony, Canon, OM System and more. With over 6 years of photography experience, her skills span across landscape and seascape photography, wildlife, astrophotography and portrait work. Her photos have been featured in a number of national magazines, including Digital Camera World and Cosmopolitan. She has also contributed to our sister site Space.com and Tech Radar, and she regularly uses binoculars and telescopes to stargaze in the dark skies of South Wales.

#6376. Rift grows among Senate Democrats over who will lead in majority

Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin hold a news conference calling for a “bold direction” for Senate Democrats on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

More Democrats emerged Tuesday wanting someone besides Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., to lead their conference in the majority.

But Schumer maintained confidence he would be reelected to the post despite Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., publicly calling for a different leader or a “concrete plan” that provides change.

“I’m confident I will be elected majority leader, and our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday. “We have great unity in our caucus, and I’ll be proud to lead it.”

Sanders said during a news conference Tuesday the election was about “change and the need for the Democratic Party to move in a new and bold direction.”

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders said, calling for an “economy that works for all, not just the people on top.”

“Do I think Chuck has been leading in that direction?” he asked. “No.”

Some incoming members and now incumbents have pointed to Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen as one possibility to challenge Schumer. Van Hollen had previously thrown cold water on the idea by saying he was instead “kicking the tires” on a presidential run in 2028 but has recently changed his tune.

A person familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking said he “has received an outpouring of calls on running for majority leader and is now in active listening mode.”

Slotkin did not endorse anyone for leader but said she had a “really productive conversation” with Van Hollen yesterday.

“Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that’s definitely different. I’m a ‘no’ until and unless I see that from anyone,” she said, urging her peers to “withhold quorum” when Senate Democrats hold their leadership elections “until you get that plan and you feel like you have a voice in that plan.”

She urged not just a roadmap for the first 100 days, but ideas for how to “communicate differently.” As for her own future, she said, “I am not actively seeking this job. I’m seeking change.”

Asked about his plans Monday evening, Van Hollen said, “It’s not about me, but I am listening to the thousands of people who have been calling for change, but especially listening to our members, with a particular ear to new members who have just come off the campaign trail.”

“What I’ve said from the very beginning is, we shouldn’t have a coronation. We should have a caucus discussion about what we're going to do with the power and responsibilities that have been invested in us,” Van Hollen said. “I’m in listening mode and haven’t shut the door.”

Van Hollen took it a step further at an event Tuesday in Washington, D.C., criticizing the minority leader and Democrats’ campaign arm over their preferences in some primaries. “Schumer and the DSCC sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC against these candidates,” he said, according to a livestream of the event.

Schumer tried to tamp down the suggestion of a rivalry. “We talk frequently, and we’re united — united in lowering costs, and united in ending this damn war,” he said of Van Hollen.

Others threw their support behind Schumer ahead of the Democratic leadership elections, which are expected to take place in December.

Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., praised Schumer for raising money and recruiting candidates like Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Roy Cooper of North Carolina to help land at minimum seven seats, and potentially nine if Alaska and Mississippi ultimately swing their way.

“That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership, and that is what Sen. Schumer has done. And that is why you will see, despite all grumblings, enormous gratitude,” she said.

Gillibrand pointed to candidates like Scott Colom, the Democrat in Mississippi who is currently leading GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a nail-biter of a race. “That wave doesn’t get created by magic. It gets created by hard work and putting the pieces together over years,” she said.

Colom, however, has been noncommittal, telling MS NOW, “Too many of our leaders are from the same areas of the country,” pointing to the Brooklyn roots of both Schumer and current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to run for speaker on the House side.

Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., said he and Schumer have had their differences. But he implied he backs him for majority leader: “At the end of the day, these are historic numbers. It’s time for us to unify. We are going to work together as a caucus to plan together about how to move forward for what the country wants us to do, and I think we have the person who I think is going to lead us there.”

Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., said Democrats have “an opportunity to do things differently, and I think we will, regardless of who the leader is. It doesn’t really matter whose name is on the door.”

“Yes,” he said of his support for Schumer, noting that so far, nobody has officially stepped up to the plate. “This is a guy that worked incredibly hard over the last couple of years. I know people have other opinions about this. But we have a mandate to do things and get things done for the American people.”

Mark Schoeff Jr., Paul M. Krawzak and Kelly Livingston contributed to this report.

#6375. The 8 Best Outdoor Security Cameras Keep an Eye on Your Home When You're Away

Security cameras ensure that you can check what's happening around your home 24/7, capturing footage and alerting you within minutes if there's a problem.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Keeping your home safe these days takes more than a deadbolt and a dog with a menacing bark. Installing a few security cameras around your property is an easy and surprisingly cost-effective way to level up your home security, adding watchful eyes that track comings and goings 24/7. Until relatively recently, the only options for personal home security were comprehensive (and expensive) systems that were installed and monitored by security professionals. Now, you can set up your own cameras and home security system that saves you cash without sacrificing performance.

Outdoor security cameras in particular are your best bet to prevent break-ins. According to Security.org, simply having a clearly visible camera or security device on your property serves as a strong deterrent for trespassers. Outdoor security cameras are equipped with features found in indoor security cameras like high-definition video, night vision, two-way audio, and more. In addition to this, they come equipped with outdoor-specific features like weather-resistant exteriors, sound detection, and integrated motion-activated spotlights.

For this guide, we got our hands on the most promising options from well-established brands including Arlo, Wyze, Ring, and Eufy and tested them at our homes and offices. Read on below to learn about the best outdoor security cameras we recommend, along with expert advice to help you choose the right option for your home and budget.

One quick note before we dive in: It’s increasingly important to pick security gear that’s compatible with whatever smart home system you already have. For example, Amazon makes it easy to pull up a live feed from your Ring camera(s) on an Echo Show or Fire TV and has designed its products to more seamlessly connect with its other smart home devices. Same goes for Google products. If you already have a few items from a major smart home brand, consider buying gear that will be as compatible as possible with it.

More Home Improvement Stories: Best Retractable Awnings ● The Popular Mechanics 2025 Yard & Garden Awards ● Best Solar-Powered Outdoor Lights

We selected our recommendations based on a round of substantial testing: We installed these cameras outdoors, and used them to survey our homes for weeks, and in some cases months. We watched them as they watched our properties, as they endured a wide spectrum of outdoor conditions including snow and rain.

We tested and compared their basic video recording functionality, evaluating them on clarity, field of view, and weather resistance as well as any special features they offer like spotlights, solar charging, sirens, and more. Some of the cameras on this list were tested in outdoor settings for months, facing a wide spectrum of outdoor conditions including snow and rain.

We also tested their more nuanced security and tech features, including motion detection notifications, AI recognition of animals and packages, two-way audio conversations, and digital borders, among others. These features were considered as well as the cost, if any, associated with buying access to all of them.

We recommended the Wyze Outdoor Cam V2 ahead of testing, based on its low price, solid specs, and the past performance of other Wyze cameras that we've tested.

The Arlo Essential XL stands out for its user-friendly design, durable exterior, and of course, its clear video quality—all for a fair price. It's completely wireless, which means you can mount it anywhere around your home without worrying about power and wiring issues.

It excels as a 24/7 outdoor cam, with features like color night vision that improves the clarity of nighttime footage. During testing, we were impressed by its resolution in low light, as well as its accurate motion detection. It provides real-time alerts directly to your smartphone, and will let you check a live feed to observe any suspicious activity live as it happens.

You can also program the integrated spotlight to automatically flash on when someone is within visual range. It's a great deterrent against potential robberies, and lets you leave the house without leaving a porch light on.

While this cam has solid features without a subscription, an Arlo Secure subscription adds cloud storage for your video footage, as well as additional target recognition and home security features, for $96 to $300 per year.

Few options balance price and quality as well as this affordable option from Wyze. The battery-operated Wyze Outdoor V2 camera can be mounted anywhere. New buyers should pick up the starter kit, which includes a base unit that allows you to expand your system with up to four cameras.

Though it's the most affordable on the list, it still offers a lineup of powerful features including motion-sensing technology that detects both body heat and movement, reducing the number of potential false alarms drastically.

The Wyze is also quite flexible for storage options with the camera capable of online cloud storage as well as localized storage on a microSD card.

Solar-powered cameras, while power-efficient, present extra setup challenges. Most of the time, the panel is attached to the body of the camera, so you need to need find to camera positions with a good field of view and get good sun exposure. Depending on the layout of your home and the surrounding area, that may lead to less-than-ideal placements, which create holes in your surveillance.

The Tapo MagCam solves this issue with a detachable solar panel, so you can keep it connected when it's effective, or remove and mount it higher above the camera to get more sun. It features a 13-foot extension cord, so you have a good amount of slack to move it to an open, sunshiny space.

Test Editor Bradley Ford mounted his test camera in a semi-shaded area, then set up the solar panel in direct sunlight. Despite the fact that he was testing at the end of 2025, when there was significantly less daily sunlight, the battery never dipped below 80 percent charge. In the warmer weather, the camera typically sat at 100 percent.

In addition, Ford preferred that the MagCam relied on local storage. "One of the things we like best is that there is no need for a subscription to access activation videos," Ford said. "They’re all stored locally on a Micro SD card in the camera. However, if you wish to pay for cloud storage, that option is also available."

This specific kit comes with a camera, solar panel, and mount, however Tapo offers others with two or three cameras as well.

Our previous pick in this category, the Ring Floodlight Cam Wired Plus, was a terrific outdoor security camera that featured a dual-LED floodlight. The new Ring Floodlight Cam Wired Pro builds on that solid design with extra features, including support for dual-band WiFi and a “bird’s-eye view” feature that tracks a recorded subject as they move within the camera’s view, showing it on a top-down layout of the area.

The camera’s 1080p video resolution and 140-degree field of view are the same as the previous model, but image quality is enhanced with high dynamic range (HDR) support, which improves visibility in both low light and extremely bright conditions.

The lights themselves are also quite bright, 2000 lumens each, and the fixtures are adjustable so you can angle the light as you please.

The Ring Floodlight Cam Wired Pro also features two-way audio support, with a 110-decibel siren that sounds when the system detects motion. It also offers customizable motion zones and 3D- motion radar for you to tailor to your property.

A word of warning: We found the wired installation was fairly difficult, so we recommend hiring an electrician unless you're experienced with wiring and up for a challenge.

Unlike any other outdoor security camera on our list, this option from Tactacam does not require a WiFi connection. Instead, it connects to cellular towers and works similarly to your smartphone. This makes the camera perfect for homes in remote locations.

The security camera does require a monthly subscription for access to on-demand videos and photos that are stored in the cloud, but plans start at just 5 bucks a month.

The device works with AA batteries or a rechargeable battery pack. In our testing, we took anywhere from two to 10 pictures a day and the pack lasted about three to four months before needing to be recharged.

In practice, the security camera is great at sensing motion more than 100 feet away, so it could potentially double as a nature cam. It lacks some of the features other, similarly priced models on this list have, but the biggest drawback is that the field of view is only about 50 feet wide.

The Arlo floodlight has everything we love from our top pick, including Arlo's superior app and software, but adds on a large floodlight, as well as a need for wired power.

As with the Arlo Essential XL, you get quality motion detection software and color night vision. Spring for Arlo Secure, and you get AI target recognition that can point out passing cars or faces, and highlight packages.

The floodlight also has some interesting features: Each light is individually adjustable, so you can angle them for the best possible coverage. That includes creative solutions like angling one light toward your back door, while pointing the other toward the steps leading to your back porch. It's a small touch, but a very appreciated one. It also includes a loud, 110-decibel siren.

If you're looking for a low-maintenance outdoor security camera system, eufy's S330 "eufycam 3" is a dynamic wireless option that supports solar charging and doesn't require professional installation.

Once installed and set up, we did not have to take either of the cameras down for recharging once over months of use. The solar panels kept them perpetually charged as long as they got exposure to a few hours of sunlight per day.

It was similarly easy to connect the cameras to the greater home security. The outdoor cameras works through the home hub which after initial installation using an ethernet cable, works comfortably through your home WiFi. The cameras can then be set up anywhere within several hundred feet of the hub without losing connection.

A big benefit we also loved is the camera system requires no monthly subscription to access its features. This includes AI-powered face recognition, customizable activity zones, and of course, motion detection.

The only drawback for this camera set is the placement of the solar panels. While the panels being integrated directly on top of the camera makes it less cumbersome, it also means you need to install them in a spot with direct sunlight or they won't properly charge.

The Reolink Argus 4 Pro gives you a sweeping 180-degree field of view, which allows you to cover large open spaces with as few cameras as possible. Properly positioned, you can achieve a near-complete view of an area with just two cameras.

This 4K camera features a dual-lens design that covers larger areas without blind spots or fishbowl-style warping. You'd think that might lead to complications with position or usage, but we found it easy to operate.

It features discrete solar panels for power, which allows for more placement flexibility: For example, you can install the camera under a ledge or rooftop, then secure the solar panel above, where it will get direct sun. That makes it easier to get the perfect shot and optimal power.

In terms of storage, the Argus 4 Pro records footage locally and connects to a home hub. You don't have to pay a monthly fee for cloud storage or additional features. Simply turn it on, connect it the hub, and in theory, it should run without issue in perpetuity.

There are two types of consumer-grade home security cameras: wireless battery-powered cameras that you can set up easily nearly anywhere, but require you to occasionally replace batteries, and wired models that connect directly to your home's electrical system.

Wired cameras are generally more expensive and require an electrician's help unless you're comfortable with home wiring, but require far less maintenance once they're installed. Their placement is also restricted to locations where you can wired them in.

Battery-powered cameras, by contrast, are only restricted by the range of your WiFi router. Of course, you'll need to access them every few months to replace their batteries. Some models feature solar panels, giving you renewable energy, but panels also impose some placement restrictions. (Namely, access to sunlight).

Wired cameras do fall short of battery-powered models in one niche scenario—when the power goes out. Unlike, say, wired smoke or carbon monoxide detectors, which have reliable battery backup, you can't count on a wired security camera to provide surveillance footage during an extended period of time if there's a power failure. It varies from model to model, but most wired cameras can only last for 30 minutes to, at most, a few hours before they go dark.

To avoid recording 24/7, which wastes power and storage space, outdoor security cameras usually feature motion sensors that trigger recording whenever there’s activity. Many cameras will also an alert to your companion app whenever they start recording.

Most cameras give you the ability to calibrate the motion sensor by setting motion zones in spots where you expect frequent false alarms, like a sidewalk. Others offer smart features that can differentiate between people, animals, and vehicles. You should also have the ability to customize your notifications, so you’ll only receive an alert in certain situations, like if it detects a person.

Furthermore, some cameras feature microphones, enabling audio detection, which can trigger recording and alerts based on nearby sounds that may be out of view (like a window breaking). Audio detection is a useful extra layer in a few specific situations, like when a single camera can’t cover the entire side of your home, but may also lead to more nuisance alerts. If you decide to use one, we recommend customizing your audio alert sensitivity if possible so you aren’t constantly getting notified when the neighbor’s dog barks.

The best outdoor security cameras record video in "Full HD" (1920 x 1080p) resolution, which captures enough detail to identify facial features or a car’s license plate. More expensive cameras record at higher resolutions, such as 2K or "Quad HD" (2560 x 1440p) or 4K Ultra HD (3840 x 2160) video, which deliver better detail. While higher resolution may help, 1080p video is usually clear enough to give you more than enough information in most situations.

Your camera’s field of view (FOV) is just as important as its resolution. Field of view refers to how wide of an angle the lens is and therefore, how much of your yard or porch is in view. With a wider FOV, your camera can see a wider area around your property, providing more coverage. For the best results, we recommend a model with a field of view between 130 and 180 degrees.

Many outdoor cameras also feature an integrated spotlight that can illuminate the surroundings if motion is detected, improving visibility in low-light situations. A spotlight also acts as a deterrent by making potential intruders more visible. Similarly, the majority of outdoor cameras offer some kind of night vision feature, which uses infrared (IR) lights to record a high-contrast black and white video in the dark. Top-of-the-line cameras are capable of recording standard video in low light, minimizing the need for night vision.

There’s no point in recording camera footage if you can’t store it for when you need it. Many manufacturers offer free cloud storage for a limited time—typically seven days–after which video is overwritten with new recordings. You can always download and save that footage, so long as you do during that initial window.

If you want to save your footage for a longer period, there are a couple of options. Many companies provide additional cloud storage for a subscription fee. There are also cameras that feature a microSD card slot for storing footage locally. This does require a bit of extra maintenance in the form of occasionally removing the card and either deleting or downloading the recorded data to free up more space on the card.

Security cameras are more than just their features. Nearly all security cameras are built to connect with other smart home devices. So, before buying any specific option, make sure it is compatible with the devices you already own. For example, Amazon makes it easy to pull up a live feed from your Ring camera(s) on an Echo Show or Fire TV. There are many brands that work with the majority of the smart home software available such as Apple, Google Nest, and Ring. Some have limited functionality on other smart home software systems outside of their brand, but still work with them. Furthermore, most security camera brands require a monthly subscription to gain full access to many of their features. These monthly subscriptions range in price and overall necessity with some basically essential to operate the cameras and store footage in the cloud while others are designed as a bonus add-on to the base product. Prior to purchase, make sure to take a close look at both the smart home compatibility as well as what comes with and without the monthly subscription service.

Most of the outdoor security cameras we recommend are sold individually or as part of a larger set. The number of cameras you need for your property will vary, based on your home security plan and how much camera coverage you want. A well-installed camera with a wide field of view can cover an important and vulnerable area on your property, such as a back door or garage.

That said, even a small home will need at least a few cameras to achieve full coverage on every ground-level door and window. You may need multiple cameras to reveal tricky blind spots created by corners, lawn features, and anything else that might impede a single camera position.

Don't freak out about needing a fleet of surveillance gear, though. Not everyone wants or needs to have every single square inch of their property under constant watch. It’s up to you to decide where you want an extra eye. The important thing is to make sure you know what you need before making a purchase.

Of course. There are no features of an outdoor security camera that would prevent it from working inside. That said, many companies make indoor cameras that are cheaper, and may feature a stand or mounting options that make more sense for blending in with your home or office.

You should always be careful when considering home security. Over the years, there have been multiple reports of strangers accessing live video feeds and recorded videos from home security cameras.

Luckily, there are simple ways to protect yourself. As with other devices, adhering to digital security best practices, such as keeping your smart home devices’ firmware up to date, creating a strong password and activating two-factor authentication wherever possible, will help prevent a breach.

You may also have concerns about who has access to video that’s stored in the cloud. Most companies ask for permission to review recordings for research and development purposes. Depending on the company, this request often comes in the form of an “opt-in” setting in the camera app, though some may turn it on by default unless you “opt out.”

Some may also share recordings with law enforcement. In some cases, they will only do so when compelled by a search warrant. A couple manufacturers, specifically Amazon (Ring) and Google (Nest), have said they will provide footage without a warrant if law enforcement claims it is an emergency.

#6373. Hidden Viruses in the Human Gut Offer New Clues to a Disorder Affecting Millions

Many gut viruses were found at lower levels in people with irritable bowel syndrome, offering new clues to a poorly understood condition that affects roughly one in ten people.

Scientists have identified more than 116,000 groups of viruses living in the human gut, over 99% of which had no close match in the largest existing catalog of gut viruses. These largely unexplored microbes could offer new clues to how the digestive system functions and why it changes in people with conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

Research into the gut microbiome has traditionally focused on bacteria, leaving much less understood about bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria. Scientists from King’s College London, Helmholtz Munich, and the University of Nottingham are now filling that gap with two studies published on November 17, 2026, in Nature Communications and Gut.

Professor Ana Valdes and Dr. Afroditi Kouraki from the University of Nottingham said, “For a long time the viral part of the gut microbiome has been a kind of dark matter: we knew it was there but couldn’t see it. Advances in sequencing and computational methods mean we can now start to map it properly, and this study shows just how much has been hidden.”

For the Nature Communications study, researchers analyzed genetic material from stool samples collected from more than 1,000 participants in TwinsUK, the largest twin registry in the United Kingdom. Using data on gut bacteria, health measurements, and diet, they examined how populations of viruses and bacteria varied together. Certain viruses were consistently more abundant alongside particular bacteria, while others showed the opposite pattern.

Dr. Panayiotis Louca, a research associate at King’s College London who led the study, said, “Gut viruses are difficult to study, so most of what we found simply isn’t in existing catalogs. What stands out is how closely they track with gut bacteria and with the chemicals those bacteria produce. We can’t yet say whether the viruses are driving that, and testing it is our next step.”

Studying twins also allowed researchers to estimate how much genetics and the environment shape the gut’s viral community. Genetic factors accounted for an estimated 47% of the variation in overall viral diversity, although most individual viral populations appeared to be influenced primarily by environmental factors.

The researchers also discovered a small group of viruses carrying genes linked to harmful bacterial behavior. These viruses were more commonly found alongside bacteria that can sometimes cause infections and less commonly alongside bacteria that break down dietary fiber.

Such relationships could be relevant to IBS, a condition that affects around 10% of the population and can significantly disrupt daily life. Its underlying causes remain poorly understood.

In the second study, published in Gut, researchers used TwinsUK data to identify 50 viral groups associated with IBS, most of which were less abundant in people with the condition. Relationships between bacteria and viruses also differed, with many viruses infecting bacteria previously linked to IBS. This suggests that the condition may involve changes across the wider microbial community rather than in bacteria alone.

Senior author Dr. Cristina Menni, who leads the metabolomics research group at the Department of Twin Research, Ageing and Genomic Epidemiology at King’s College London, said, “Our research highlights that to fully understand the gut microbiome and its links to health and disease, we need to look beyond bacteria and consider the viruses that live alongside them. We reveal a fascinating and largely unexplored dimension of the gut microbiome—discovering that viruses are not only closely associated with bacterial communities, but also with the metabolites that connect the microbiome to our health. This opens exciting new avenues for understanding how the gut ecosystem works.”

Future research will examine whether gut viruses actively influence bacterial metabolism and how these interactions change in health and disease. Understanding these relationships could eventually help researchers develop better biological markers and treatments for IBS, as well as more personalized approaches to gut health.

Dr. Louca added: “The study is observational, so it cannot show that the viruses cause these effects, but it provides greater understanding of a largely unexplored area of the human gut. It would also be beneficial to replicate the study on a more diverse cohort, as participants were mostly older women of European ancestry.”

“Population-level characterization of the human gut phageome and its association with microbial metabolites” by Panayiotis Louca, Mohammadali Khan Mirzaei, Afroditi Kouraki, Erfan Khamespanah, Yu Lin, Xue Peng, Robert Pope, Alessia Visconti, Francesco Asnicar, Daniel Kirk, Ricardo Costeira, Nicola Segata, Mario Falchi, Jordana T. Bell, Tim D. Spector, Lindsey A. Edwards, Li Deng, Ana M. Valdes and Cristina Menni, 17 November 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79230-0

#6370. Semiconductor Breakthrough Cracks a Longstanding Solar Energy Problem

An unusual material could help us make better use of the sun’s energy, offering new possibilities for more efficient solar power and fuel production.

Generating more electricity from sunlight does not necessarily mean installing more solar panels. Finding ways to extract more energy from the light that already reaches them could make solar power a more practical source of electricity. Part of the challenge lies in what happens inside a solar cell in the moments after it absorbs sunlight.

Solar cells contain materials called semiconductors, which use the energy from sunlight to free negatively charged electrons, leaving behind positively charged gaps known as holes. Both charges must be collected to generate electricity. If an electron and a hole meet and cancel each other out, a process known as recombination, the energy they carry is lost. Unfortunately, materials that are particularly good at absorbing sunlight also tend to lose these charges more quickly.

A study led by the University of Oxford has identified a promising exception in a semiconductor called bismuth sulfide. Published October 28, 2026, in Nature, the research examined how the material’s unusual electronic structure could help overcome this longstanding limitation in solar energy technology.

To investigate how long electrical charges survive in bismuth sulfide, the researchers exposed thin films of the material to extremely short laser pulses. They then tracked how quickly the charges disappeared using a technique called ultrafast terahertz spectroscopy, conducting measurements at temperatures ranging from room temperature to just above absolute zero.

“One of the longstanding challenges in developing efficient solar-energy materials is that the properties which make a semiconductor very good at absorbing sunlight also tend to make the resulting electrical charges disappear quickly,” said corresponding author Professor Laura Herz (Department of Physics, University of Oxford). “Our work shows that this trade-off is not inevitable. By uncovering how an unusual electronic structure can combine strong light absorption with much slower recombination, we have identified a new principle for designing semiconductors that could help us harvest solar energy more efficiently.”

Electronic structure calculations by Professor Marina Filip’s group in Oxford’s Department of Physics helped explain why bismuth sulfide behaves differently. The material has two closely spaced routes through which electrons can move between energy levels. One allows the material to absorb light strongly, while the other sits at a slightly lower energy and allows charges to disappear much more slowly. Because the two are so close together, charges spend much of their time in the lower-energy states, which effectively serve as a temporary storage reservoir.

Cooling the material provided further evidence for this explanation. In most semiconductors, electrical charges disappear faster as temperatures drop. In bismuth sulfide, more charges settled into the reservoir as the material cooled, allowing them to survive longer. The results matched the team’s model of what physicists call a pseudo-direct semiconductor.

Even at room temperature, the researchers estimate that this arrangement reduces the rate of charge loss by about 75% compared with conventional semiconductors that absorb light equally well.

Giving electrical charges more time to be collected could improve the efficiency of solar panels without compromising their ability to capture sunlight. The benefits could also extend beyond electricity generation. Longer-lived charges could provide more time for the chemical reactions needed to produce fuels using sunlight.

“What makes this discovery particularly exciting is that we are not simply improving an existing semiconductor property but identifying a different way in which semiconductors can behave,” said Professor Herz. “Understanding this mechanism gives us a roadmap for discovering and potentially engineering other materials with similarly advantageous properties.”

The team’s calculations suggest that researchers could search existing materials databases for semiconductors with similar properties or engineer new ones. However, the study demonstrates the underlying physical mechanism rather than the performance of a finished solar cell. Further research will be needed to determine how these properties can be put to use in solar energy technologies.

Reference: “Delayed electron–hole recombination in a pseudo-direct semiconductor” by Marcello Righetto, Debalina Banerjee, Zhenglin Jia, Joshua R. S. Lilly, Vincent J. -Y. Lim, Snigdha Lal, Siyu Yan, Jae Eun Lee, Jay B. Patel, Michael B. Johnston, Qianqian Lin, Marina R. Filip and Laura M. Herz, 28 October 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11223-x

At a cliff site in Texas, archaeologists discovered hundreds of bison bones, stone tools and arrowheads, suggesting Indigenous people used "bison jumps" to hunt.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have uncovered an extremely rare example of a "bison jump" in the Texas Panhandle, where a natural geological formation allowed Indigenous people to hunt North America's largest living land mammal for 3,000 years. The discovery confirms that the prehistoric hunting technique ‪—‬ which involved channeling a herd of bison into a stampede off a cliff, akin to "walking the plank" ‪—‬ was not limited to the northern Plains like experts previously thought.

"Bison jumping is an iconic, uniquely North American hunting technique that yielded some of the most productive food-getting events in the history of human hunting," researchers wrote in a study published online Nov. 9 in the journal American Antiquity.

Although jump sites are well known throughout the northern Plains, only one such site had ever been found in the southern Plains. But a second bison jump called Nighthawk has now been identified in Caprock Canyons State Park in the Texas Panhandle, and researchers found that Indigenous people used the Nighthawk bison jump for millennia.

"Returning to the same place over and over again over 3,000 years shows that people had a significant connection to the Nighthawk hunting facility," study first author Gus Costa, an archaeologist at Rice University in Houston, said in a statement.

Nighthawk was found when bison remains began eroding from a bone bed (a place where bones naturally accumulate) underneath a roughly 65-foot-tall (20 meters) cliff spur. Archaeologists investigated and found chipped stone tools near the bones, as well as a few arrowheads. Several of the bison bones had cut marks from stone tools consistent with prehistoric butchery practices. These discoveries added up to a possible bison jump.

Archaeologists found hundreds of bison bones at the Nighthawk bison jump site in Texas.

"The only way bison can arrive at the site is by falling from above, as the site surface is sandwiched between two cliffs," the researchers wrote. Indigenous hunters likely used the cliff's natural spur shape to herd the bison to their deaths. "Instead of a stampede toward a surprise fall, Nighthawk could have operated more like 'walking the plank,'" according to the researchers.

Even more surprising than the discovery of a bison jump site in the southern Plains was the length of time the jump was used.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A series of radiocarbon dates revealed that there were at least seven mass bison kills at Nighthawk over a span of three millennia, between roughly 1550 B.C. and A.D. 1550. One of these events, which the researcher named Kill 3, was responsible for most of the bison bones. That enormously successful hunt most likely took place around A.D. 300 to 400 and would have required an immense labor force and precise coordination.

Archaeologists excavating a bison jump site called Nighthawk in Caprock Canyons State Park in the Texas Panhandle.

"Bison jumping is a complicated community effort," Costa said. "Large scale bison harvests (like jumps) are exciting because they require a large group of people working together to be successful."

It is not entirely clear what the Indigenous hunters were doing with the bison killed in the hunt. In the northern Plains, archaeologists have long assumed that bison jumps were generally performed in the fall and used to provision the community for winter. Bison in the North were used to make pemmican, a shelf-stable mix of dried meat and rendered fat.

But although pemmican was an extremely useful foodstuff and trade good in the North, it was likely too warm in Texas for bison fat to last more than a few weeks, the researchers wrote. This may mean that the southern Plains bison hunts were more useful for displaying power and building alliances.

All of the kill events at Nighthawk were at least a century apart, with an average of 500 years between each bison jump. That points to an infrequent use of the jump but also a clear memory of its utility.

"The simplest explanation for long-lived jump facilities is that these techniques were passed down over long time spans rather than revived again and again," the researchers wrote.

Costa, A. G., Houk, B. A., Lyle, A. S., Bement, L., Lintz, C., Lawrence, K. L., Frederick, C. D., & Culleton, B. J. (2026). The Nighthawk bison jump: New evidence for recurrent Late Holocene bison jumping in the Southern Plains. American Antiquity, 1–28. https://doi.org/10.1017/aaq.2026.10229
