#6305. An overlooked brain region offers new clues to how memory works

In mice, a thin brain sheet called the claustrum kept a smell or a touch in working memory for 30 seconds, and quieting it cut performance.

Anyone following a conversation holds the last sentence in mind while the next one arrives. The sound is gone within a moment, yet the brain keeps using it for seconds, and where it keeps it is only partly understood.

Part of that job, at least in mice, belongs to a sliver of nerve cells wedged between the cortex and the structures beneath it.

The sliver is called the claustrum. In mice, it kept a trace of a smell or a touch for up to 30 seconds. Quieting it cut the animals’ scores on a memory task by roughly 40% to 60%.

Alan Carleton and Ivan Rodriguez of the University of Geneva led the work, with Anindya Bhattacharjee as first author.

Carleton’s lab in the Department of Basic Neurosciences studies how the brain handles the senses, and the claustrum caught the team’s attention because of its wiring.

“Its neurons are connected to almost all regions of the cortex, which puts it in a good position to receive and influence information from very different networks,” Carleton said.

The short-term hold the study tested is called working memory. Reading and deciding both depend on it, and it is impaired in disorders such as schizophrenia and ADHD.

It runs on brain circuits spread across many regions, and how those circuits hold information over time isn’t clear.

The team trained head-fixed mice on a game of same or different.

A tone marked the start of each trial. Then came a one-second cue. It was one of two odors, or a puff of air on the left or right whiskers.

After a delay of 5 to 60 seconds, a second cue arrived. If it differed from the first, the mouse earned a drop of water by licking a tube. If it matched, licking earned nothing.

Thirty mice learned the odor version, and within about 400 trials they were scoring above 70%. Twenty-three of the 25 mice given the whisker version learned it too.

Scores fell as the delay grew. The memory faded at the same rate for both senses, with a half-life of about 20 seconds in the typical mouse.

In seven mice, the team watched claustrum cells through a tiny lens while the animals played. Each cell carried a sensor that glows when the cell is active.

About a quarter of the cells fired at the cue, and about 60% fired during the wait. Roughly a quarter responded to one cue but not the other.

The cells’ activity shifted as the wait went on. Even so, a computer program reading the whole population could still tell which cue the mouse had received, right up to the second cue, at every delay tested.

On trials the mouse got wrong, the program did far worse.

“Far from being a static memory, neuronal activity changed over time,” Rodriguez said. “Nevertheless, the identity of the stimulus remained sufficiently present to be decoded up to 30 seconds later.”

Only a small share of the cells tracked licking or movements of the nose, mouth or forepaw, about 8% at most for any one of them.

The findings suggest that the memory trace was not simply a reflection of the animal’s movements.

To test whether the claustrum was needed, the team dialed its cells down in two ways. A drug that acts only on cells carrying an engineered receptor cut scores by about 40%.

Optogenetics, in which cells carry a light-sensitive protein and a fiber delivers light for about one second, cut them by 40% to 60%.

The light trials were mixed in with ordinary trials in the same session, and performance suffered regardless of when the light was delivered.

Dimming the claustrum during the first cue, early in the wait, late in the wait or during the second cue hurt in every case.

“The result was similar regardless of the type of stimulus, olfactory or tactile, and regardless of when the disruption occurred during the waiting period between the two stimuli,” Carleton said.

Mice carrying a harmless protein instead of the light-sensitive one played as well with the light on as off.

The same mice then played a version with no delay, telling two odors or two puffs apart on the spot. The light had no effect on that.

The mice’s pupils, body movements and licking looked the same with and without it, and they didn’t lick early during long waits. What fell was the rate of correct licks on trials where the cues differed.

“Disrupting the claustrum specifically impairs the ability to use temporarily held information to guide behavior, without affecting perception itself,” Carleton said.

The sliver is thin and poorly bounded, so the team could only partly quiet it, and the mice still scored well above chance. Other regions carry short-term memories too, and this study doesn’t say how the work is shared.

A second team reported in June on a set of cells in and around the claustrum that connect to the prefrontal cortex. Mice needed those cells while holding a location in mind in a maze.

Silencing them during the decision itself improved performance, the opposite of what the Geneva team saw.

The two groups used different tasks and targeted different cells, and neither result settles which cells do what.

How the claustrum keeps a memory steady while its own activity drifts is the open question.

The next step, Carleton said, is to work out how the claustrum talks to the cortex, and how that exchange keeps a held memory from degrading.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

Quantinuum's Helios processor achieved a record-low failure rate of just 0.0005%, suggesting fault-tolerant quantum systems may need far fewer qubits than previously thought.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists at Quantinuum say they've set a new record in quantum error correction that brings large-scale, fault-tolerant systems one step closer.

The team claims their 98-qubit quantum system, Helios, demonstrated a failure rate of just 0.0005% in tests of its quantum memory, which is equivalent to an estimated five uncorrectable errors per million rounds of error checking.

This rate bests the previous benchmark set by Google's 105-qubit Willow quantum chip, which demonstrated an estimated 772 uncorrectable errors per million rounds in comparable tests, for an error rate of 0.0772%.

The result brings quantum computing closer to the "megaquop regime," where systems can run over a million operations without encountering an error, the researchers said. They detailed their findings in a study uploaded Oct. 16 to the arXiv preprint server.

In a statement, Robin Blume-Kohout, co-director of Sandia National Laboratories' Quantum Performance Lab, called the achievement "a significant milestone that quantum computing researchers have been working toward for many years."

"A scaled-up version of this system could reach the reliability required for useful fault-tolerant computation at a feasible size — less than a million physical qubits — which improves the outlook for practical quantum computing," added Blume-Kohout, who was not involved in the research.

Preserving the fragile information stored in qubits is one of quantum computing's greatest challenges and presents a major barrier to making systems practical.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Qubits, the most basic units of quantum information, are extremely sensitive to interference. Their delicate quantum states can be easily disturbed by heat, vibrations and other forms of environmental "noise," and if this happens in the middle of a calculation, the result becomes far less reliable — if it survives at all.

Quantum error correction has become a focal point for researchers for this exact reason. It introduces redundancy to quantum systems to ensure that small, potentially manageable errors don't wipe out entire calculations.

This involves spreading quantum information across multiple physical qubits to form a "logical" qubit. If a single qubit loses its quantum state due to interference, the redundancy provided by the logical qubit helps to keep the information it collectively stores intact.

The challenge is packing enough qubits into computers to ensure redundancy for longer, more complex calculations. This presents something of a catch-22: Adding more qubits provides more redundancy, allowing for larger quantum systems, but it also increases the opportunity for errors.

Unlike Google's Willow processor, which is based on superconducting circuits, Helios uses electrically charged barium ions that can be dynamically rearranged.

By shuttling ions around the processor, scientists can unite different pairs of qubits, allowing them to exchange information directly. That way, it doesn't have to pass through multiple qubits — a process that can introduce additional errors.

The team also developed a technique called "leakage repumping," which uses precise, split-second laser pulses to bring qubits that have slipped out of their information-storing quantum state back into a usable state.

To test how effectively Helios could correct errors as more physical qubits were added, the researchers used a type of error-correcting code known as a color code. They tested three progressively larger versions ‪—‬ known as code distances 3, 5 and 7 ​​—‬ which could correct one, two and three physical-qubit errors, respectively.

They found that Helios became substantially more reliable as they added more physical qubits. Each increase in code distance reduced the likelihood of an uncorrectable error by roughly 12 times. At the highest level tested (distance 7), Helios achieved a record failure rate of approximately one uncorrectable error per 200,000 rounds.

In the study, which has not been peer-reviewed yet, the scientists suggested that future quantum computers using the same technology as Helios could achieve extremely low error rates without needing an impractically high number of physical qubits.

According to estimates from Quantinuum representatives, a future trapped-ion system could support 100 logical qubits using approximately 30,000 physical qubits, compared with around 900,000 for a competing superconducting system.

"There is still substantial engineering ahead to scale to much larger systems and integrate all the elements of fault-tolerant computation, but this work demonstrates that our underlying hardware and error-correction approach can deliver the exponential improvement in reliability that large-scale quantum computers will depend upon," Dave Hayes, director of computational design and theory at Quantinuum, told Live Science in an email.

The researchers said they plan to apply their latest findings to Quantinuum's upcoming quantum

#6302. Violent star collisions may have created the earliest giant black holes

Crowded early star clusters could merge stars into one giant, and a new model shows how that giant may become a black hole seed.

Space is so empty that two stars almost never hit each other. In the first star clusters, though, stars were packed so tightly that they may have crashed into one another again and again.

A new model suggests those crashes could merge stars until one carried the mass of the whole cluster. A star that heavy may have no way to die except by collapsing into a black hole.

That matters because the James Webb Space Telescope keeps finding enormous black holes far earlier in cosmic history than astronomers expected.

The new work, led by Claire Williams, a doctoral student at UCLA, is a calculation rather than an observation. It maps where colliding stars could have made the seeds of those black holes.

Webb’s deep images show extremely compact star clusters in the early universe, and computer simulations of that era produce the same crowding.

Williams and her colleagues in the UCLA Division of Astronomy and Astrophysics built a model to ask what happens to the stars inside them.

Co-authors of the study came from Northwestern’s CIERA and seven other institutions.

The model clusters ranged from about two-thirds of a light-year in radius to roughly 300 light-years.

They held anywhere from ten thousand to a billion times the mass of the Sun. Some had a black hole at the center and some did not.

For each one, the team worked out how often stars would run into each other before something stopped them. That could be the stars burning out or a neighboring clump of matter crashing in.

Even with the strictest assumptions, collisions should have been common in many of these systems. Test simulations tracking 1,000 individual stars near a cluster’s center agreed on where they happen.

In an interview with Earth.com, Williams said star collisions matter today only in rare, extreme places, such as the cores of galaxies. So astronomers usually don’t treat them as central to how stars live.

“We were surprised to discover how ubiquitous these collisions might have been,” she said.

What a collision does depends on how fast the two stars meet. If they meet at speeds below the escape speed at a star’s surface, they can merge into one bigger star.

At higher speeds, collisions can strip material from both stars or destroy them entirely, releasing gas from their interiors.

In a cluster with no black hole, the model found no system where stars moved fast enough to destroy each other. Every collision was a merger.

And because the merged stars are heavier than their neighbors, they sink toward the center quickly, where they collide again.

“Perhaps the strangest outcome of our simulations is that stars can merge repeatedly within the cluster until they form one gigantic star with a mass equal to that of an entire cluster,” Williams said.

“When a star this huge reaches the end of its life, models suggest that it may have no option but to collapse into itself and form a massive black hole.”

How big that merged star gets depends mostly on how tightly the cluster is packed.

In the model’s standard setup, the central star passes 200 times the Sun’s mass only once a cluster holds roughly 100,000 suns’ worth of stars per cubic parsec. A parsec is about 3.3 light-years.

Above that line, nearly all of the lightest clusters in the model produced one. In the densest cases, the merged star passed 100,000 solar masses.

When the team filled the clusters with heavy stars instead of Sun-like ones, only 22 systems built a giant at all, and the largest reached 512 solar masses. Heavy stars burn out quickly, so the collisions ran out of time.

If each giant collapses into a black hole of the same mass, the result is an intermediate-mass black hole, a size astronomers have struggled to find.

Other groups have already proposed stellar mergers as a route to early black holes, and the team’s giant-star masses broadly agree with theirs.

The new part is one framework that runs from an ordinary early cluster to a black hole star wrapped in gas.

Once a black hole is at the center, the outcome changes. Its gravity speeds up the stars closest to it, so collisions there happen too fast to merge.

The stars are torn apart instead, and the gas from their interiors piles up in a tiny region around the black hole.

The Milky Way’s center is the nearby example. “One place in the nearby universe where collisions between stars are common is the galactic center,” Williams said.

“In our model, once these very massive stars turn into intermediate-mass black holes, the system resembles our own galactic center, which is a black hole surrounded by a dense star cluster.”

That dense, gassy core is why the authors connect the model to Webb’s little red dots.

Astronomers believe these compact objects hold a rapidly growing black hole, and several recent studies describe that black hole as buried in dense gas.

In the model, a cluster as dense as a little red dot would build a central star of 10,000 to 100,000 solar masses. Once a black hole formed, collisions would keep feeding gas toward it.

Williams said other researchers had already proposed that very massive stars might be connected to the dots.

“Little Red Dots may represent the densest extreme of a continuum of stellar systems that formed naturally in the early Universe, rather than an entirely separate class of object,” she told Earth.com.

Smadar Naoz, a UCLA astrophysicist and co-author, compared the research on the dots to the tale of blind people each describing an elephant by the part they touch.

“Our research connects several of those perspectives together and may help us see more of the elephant,” Naoz said.

Asked by Earth.com what Webb could see to confirm the picture, Williams said there may not be a single “smoking gun.”

The most direct test, she said, is spectroscopy, which splits an object’s light into its component wavelengths.

The bright and dark lines in that spectrum reveal the temperature, chemical makeup and motion of the material giving off the light.

With better theoretical predictions, those lines could help tell light from very massive stars apart from light reworked by gas around a black hole that is actively feeding.

One clue would be unusual amounts of certain elements, thrown out when collisions expose the insides of stars. The gas from these collisions may be unusually rich in nitrogen, which has already turned up in some early clusters.

A second test would look for leftovers. If collisions built very massive stars that later collapsed, some of the resulting black holes may now wander near the edges of galaxies.

In a newer preprint that has not been peer reviewed, Williams’s team reports that upcoming sky surveys could find them.

Surveys by the Rubin Observatory and the Roman Space Telescope may spot the black holes when they destroy stars that pass too close.

“Finding a larger population of these events would provide independent evidence that dense early clusters formed intermediate-mass black holes through runaway stellar collisions,” Williams said.

The authors list what their simplified model leaves out. It ignores any gas left over from the cluster’s birth, which they expect would pull merged stars inward even faster.

It doesn’t update the stars’ masses as mergers happen, so it may miss runaway growth.

Its estimate of how much material a fast collision strips from a star is also likely too high. So the gas densities around black holes may be overstated.

The model also stops at the giant star. It doesn’t follow whether that star collapses, how much of its mass ends up inside a black hole, or how fast the black hole grows afterward.

Williams said the team’s next step is following the gas that fast collisions throw into the middle of a cluster. The current model estimates how much gas that makes, but not where it goes.

The gas could stay trapped, cool and feed the black hole, change the orbits of nearby stars, or be driven out. Each outcome would leave a different signature for telescopes to look for.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal.

#6301. The 6 Best Portable Generators Give You Power Whenever and Wherever You Need It

These editor-tested models are ideal for camping, tailgating, or powering tools when you’re too far from an outlet.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Generators come in all sizes, but when you need power for camping or tailgating, or to power tools when you’re too far from an outlet, a large one meant for home backup is just too much. Power stations are handy, but once they run out of power, they take a long time to recharge. That’s where a smaller-sized portable generator can really shine. So long as you have the fuel, they can keep running.

When you’re shopping for a portable generator, there are a few important things to consider, including power, weight, and fuel type. For portable power, models that output 2,000 to 5,000 watts will generally be simple enough to lift in and out of a truck, though some models that generate more are designed to be lightweight. Anything over 100 pounds starts to buck the idea of something being portable, even if it has wheels.

Fuel type matters, too. All generators run on gas, but dual-fuel models can also run on propane. The drawback is that propane delivers slightly less power output and shorter running time, but it runs a lot cleaner and is much less messy to deal with.

If you’re powering sensitive electronics like digital equipment or TVs, you’ll also want to look for an inverter generator, which delivers more stable “cleaner” power that won’t damage your gear. They also run quieter than standard models. For these reasons, all of the picks on our list are inverter generators.

Keeping portability in mind, the models we cover in this story are all 7,500 watts and under. For the models that we tested, we based our methods on our experience using generators for backup power with and without transfer switches, on construction sites to run power tools and equipment, as well as running sound systems and lighting at outdoor events. We measured the sound levels of these generators idling with no load, and while running under load at two feet and 25 feet. We then used an oscilloscope to observe the sine wave of the alternating current generated by these machines, and a clamp meter to check voltage output.

Some examples of devices we used with large starting and running loads include a large air conditioner and a portable table saw. In one case, we even tested it paired to a solar inverter-charger. We evaluated these generators based on ease of starting, power response, sound levels, value, safety, and reliability to select the top performers.

The Honda EU2200i inverter generator has just about everything you want from a portable generator. It’s half the size and weight of comparable generators in its class; it’s very quiet and clean when operating; and it’s fully enclosed so you can quickly and easily transport it and move it around without worrying about it getting caught on anything.

That enclosure is an important feature, as it protects the inverter electronics and helps contain noise—the EU2200i is remarkably quiet. In testing, we measured sound levels of 68.9 decibels at the generator under no load. When we switched it to “eco” mode, which reduces engine speed when power isn’t called for, the sound was reduced to 76 decibels.

When we used an oscilloscope to look at the sine wave of the current generated, the curves were smooth and symmetrical, an indicator of “clean” power. This remained true even when running heavy loads from devices like a table saw or an air conditioner.

There are some nice design features, too. The vent on the gas cap closes so fumes or fuel cannot escape. You could breathe freely packing this in the passenger compartment of an SUV. Likewise, the power on/off switch doubles as a fuel shutoff, so it can’t be forgotten.

Lastly, the EU2200i has ports for parallel operation. With the correct cable kit, it connects to a second EU2200i to double the output to 4,400 starting and 3,600 running watts. The EU2200i is ideal for camping and other outdoor events where generator noise might be frowned on.

We like the GD400BN because it’s powerful, quiet, and portable at a reasonable price point. The interesting thing about this inverter generator is how much power it can deliver, yet it’s still as compact as similar generators that deliver half as much output. Even when running on lower-output propane as the fuel source, it can run up to 3,000 watts, which is considerable for a generator that only weighs 47 pounds.

Another plug or two would’ve been nice, however. Its single AC outlet limits you to plugging one power tool or appliance at a time, despite having enough output to power more than one device. It does have a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet for connecting to an RV, though, so that does make up for it a bit, but only if you have that need. The 1.1-gallon fuel tank is also a bit limiting regarding runtime for gasoline, but that’s easily overcome by using propane. For all intents and purposes, this is a very nice dual-fuel generator, and at a list price of $600, it comes at a reasonable price to boot.

The Wen DF360iX offers a considerable amount of utility for an affordable price. You have the option to run the generator on gasoline or propane with a running output of up to 2,900 watts. While propane delivers a bit less at 2,600 watts, that’s plenty of power for a job site or camping use and even enough electricity for small to midsize RVs.

While this generator is fairly light at 49 pounds, it doesn’t cut back on ports, including a 30-amp port for direct connection to an RV. There are also two three-prong AC ports, a 12-volt DC receptacle, and two USB-A ports. Like most inverter generators, it produces less noise. This model is rated at around 65 decibels of noise at a quarter load, which is quiet enough that it shouldn’t bother the neighbors. There are some nice safety features, too, including auto-shutoff if the fuel runs too low and a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor that detects if dangerous levels are present.

Of course, with any generator in this price range (under $500), there are compromises. This model has a pretty small fuel tank—only 1.5 gallons—so you won’t be able to run this on gasoline for long periods (around five hours with a half-load) without having to stop and refill. You can mitigate this, however, by relying on a larger tank of propane. For example, a 20-pound tank should enable you to run it for up to 14 hours.

GENERATOR SAFETYWhile not hard to run, generators present dangers, so you need to follow basic safety rules. Never operate them in a closed space, like a garage or shed. Exhaust gases contain carbon monoxide (CO), a lethal, odorless, colorless gas. Most manufacturers offer models that shut down when they detect carbon monoxide building up. Do not run a generator in a garage with the door open, or in front of the garage with the door open, because carbon monoxide can still get trapped and seep into the house. Run generators at least 20 feet away, including from windows and doors, with the exhaust blowing away from the house.

RV owners need a generator outfitted with at least a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet, but it also helps to have a decent amount of power to go with it, so that you can run things like a heater or an air conditioner. This model from Champion offers both, with the outlet and up to 3,500 running watts, which is enough to power a small- to medium-sized RV.

It also offers great fuel flexibility. With a full 2.3-gallon fuel tank, it should be able to run for up to 14 hours, but it’s dual-fuel, so with a full 20-pound propane tank, this generator can supply 21 hours of uninterrupted power.

In addition to being a solid companion for camping and RVing, this generator could serve as a useful tool in an emergency at home where power is needed. Using a manual transfer switch, you could power a few 120-volt circuits using the 30-amp connection. And the inverter will help to keep it running more quietly, which is helpful at home or the campground.

One of our test editors picked up this generator when faced with a home emergency where he needed a generator with specific features, quickly, and on a budget. A failed generator at a solar-powered off-grid cabin necessitated the quick acquisition, and, happily, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel Inverter Generator showed up on the doorstep in only two days.

In about 15 minutes, with minimal assembly and after adding oil, the generator was connected to a propane cylinder by a hose and was running on the first cycle of the starter. Since then, it’s run steadily at 500 watts, up to 5,500 watts, at 240 volts (great for powering high-voltage appliances like dryers or water pumps), to charge a battery bank during the winter when sunlight wasn’t enough to get the job done.

This Pulsar puts out very clean power, too, with a claimed total harmonic distortion (THD) of less than 3 percent, which met the requirements of the solar inverter-charger it was paired with.

Using the inverter to monitor the current frequency, we found that it was indeed very stable with minimal variance, between 59.97 and 60.09 Hz. All things considered, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel is a good value for the specs, capacity, and features.

Generac’s iQ3800 Portable Inverter Generator is a great example of what we love about dual-fuel, inverter generators. This type of generator can deliver cleaner power than a standard model, meaning there’s less distortion in the electrical current frequency. That’s ideal for powering sensitive electronics, such as TVs, computer equipment, and smart household appliances. This is also a closed-frame inverter generator, which tends to be quieter; the iQ3800 is one of the quietest generators we’ve tested of this size.

We were very impressed with how easy the iQ3800 is to operate. The electric start and auto choke worked perfectly, taking only about four to five seconds, while the manual pull-start also fired up the generator with minimal effort. Switching between fuel types was also very simple to perform. Once running, you can view important information on an easy-to-read LED display that lists the total hours the machine has run, the fuel level for the gasoline tank (there’s no gauge for propane), and a load gauge that uses a bar graph to show power output level—knowing that helps to avoid overloading the generator.

The inverter technology might be the most important feature of the iQ3800. This generator has a total harmonic distortion (THD)—a level of variance in the current frequency—of less than 3 percent, which is very low. Essentially, anything with a screen or any smart device would be best powered using an inverter generator like the iQ3800. It’s an ideal generator to power RVs in campgrounds or off-grid, and a great option for emergency backup in urban areas.

Full Generac iQ3800 Portable Inverter Generator Review

These generators, sometimes called backup generators, are used to provide temporary power when and where it is needed. Portable is a relative term; some are more portable than others. While the smallest models can be picked up and carried, most have wheels and a handle to make transport easier. However, at 100 pounds or more, picking them up to load or move may take two people. Appliances, power tools, or other devices can be plugged directly into standard outlets on the generator’s front panel.

Additionally, many models have a twist-lock plug that can provide up to 240 volts and be used to power circuits in a home via a manual transfer switch. You may hear generators like these referred to as “open frame” generators, which simply means that the engine, fuel tank, and generator components are not enclosed in bodywork.

Though inverter-type generators are—like their standard cousins—typically portable, we group them separately because they’re significantly and technically different in terms of how they work.

Like most generators, inverter generators provide 120/240 volts of AC power. They generate AC current just like the others, but it’s then converted to DC (Direct Current), and then inverted back to AC. The conversion and inversion is controlled by circuitry which acts like a filter, flattens surges, and cleans up the sine wave (or oscillating wave) of the electrical current.

Typical generators have varying degrees of distortion in the sine wave of the alternating current. This isn’t usually an issue for most electrical devices, though sensitive electronics like tablets, laptops, televisions, and other smart devices can be damaged by current distortion or surges. These devices will last longer with “clean” power and steady voltage. Because of that added complication, inverter generators can be significantly more expensive.

Standby generators are permanently installed and connected to a home. These may power selected, critical circuits during a power outage, or may provide power for the whole home. Standby generators have systems that monitor power supplied by a utility and start automatically in the event of an outage. Since they’re not portable or easily moved, we didn’t include any here.

It’s important to know what you intend to power with a generator in order to choose the right size. Manufacturers list two figures for generators: starting watts and running watts. Starting watts include the initial surge required to start appliances or tools with powerful electric motors or compressors. Once started, these devices require far less power to run continuously.

Many manufacturers have a chart with estimated power requirements for common appliances and tools to help you figure out what you need. For a more precise measurement, you can also calculate the figure yourself by adding up the power consumption of specific appliances and adding them together.

To calculate watts, multiply voltage (usually 120 volts) by the amps (amperage) required to run the appliance (usually found on a tag attached to the appliance). Do this for each item that the generator will power.

Most portable generators are powered by gasoline, the most commonly available fuel. However, when using generators for emergency power, their infrequent use presents some issues to consider.

The first is that when big, catastrophic storms hit and power outages last for days, gas stations may struggle to meet demand, resulting in long lines. The second issue has to do with the infrequent use of backup generators, which may sit for months to years between uses.

Gasoline sitting in a carburetor will slowly evaporate over time, leaving gummy deposits that can block fuel from getting through, making it difficult or even impossible to start your generator without servicing. You can avoid this by closing the fuel valve and letting the generator run until it stalls, using up the remaining fuel in the carburetor. Also, over time, gasoline can oxidize or become “stale,” losing combustibility. It may also absorb water, which can then corrode fuel tanks and other metal components in the fuel system. Starting a generator regularly, as well as treating fuel with a stabilizer, can help fight these issues.

Ethanol-free gasoline, available at some gas stations, is also less susceptible to degradation over time than standard 87-octane pump gas; however, it’s still a good idea to mix the fuel going into your generator with stabilizer.

Dual-fuel generators can run on gasoline or liquified petroleum gas (LPG), commonly known as propane. Switching between the fuels is simple, and you won’t be tied to the availability of one type of fuel.

A big advantage of propane is that it’s very stable when stored for long periods of time. It won’t go stale, and it won’t gum up carburetors from sitting. Plus, some homes that use propane for other purposes may already have large storage tanks on the premises, foregoing the need to make repeated trips out for fuel.

The downside to propane is that it creates fewer BTUs (British Thermal Units, a measurement of energy) than the same amount of gasoline. So, a generator running on propane will have slightly reduced starting and running watts. On the plus side, though, it will also run a little quieter than those that run on gasoline.

While not as common, tri-fuel generators add an option to connect by natural gas. Some propane-powered generators can be converted to run on natural gas, as well. Like propane, natural gas can run cleaner and a little quieter. However, it also creates fewer BTUs than gasoline and propane, so it will also produce reduced starting and running watts.

Natural gas also requires a dedicated line for the generator, which most homes that have access to natural gas will not have, and thus will need to be professionally installed.

If you’re powering appliances, tools, or other devices by plugging them directly into the standard outlets on the generator, the answer is no. If the generator is being used to power circuits in your home, maybe. It’s always best to consult the operator’s manual, a licensed electrician, or your local building officials about township ordinances—some localities may have requirements that differ from the National Electrical Code (NEC).

Electrical circuits need to be grounded to operate devices safely, so that any current that shorts out or has a fault is directed to the ground, i.e., the actual, literal earth, so the user doesn’t become the conduit to “ground.”

There are two ways that generators are grounded: neutral-bonded and floating neutral. Neutral-bonded means the neutral wire is connected (i.e., bonded) to the generator frame. With a floating neutral, the neutral is not connected to the frame. In the latter case, the generator should be grounded by connecting the ground terminal to a grounding rod driven into the ground.

Generators with ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) outlets, when used to power circuits in your home, require neutral switching and a manual transfer switch, and must be grounded by connecting the ground terminal to a ground rod driven into the soil. Neutral-switching transfer switches are also referred to as three-pole transfer switches.

There could be numerous reasons for difficulty starting a generator. The first things to check are whether or not there's any fuel in the tank, and if the fuel valve is turned open. Then, check for any obstructions in the air cleaner box. If that’s clean, move on to check that the engine has spark.

If your generator has sat for a long time without treated fuel, the carburetor may be clogged up and require cleaning—if you’re unfamiliar with any of these steps, it may be best to take it to a shop for service.

In an emergency, use what you can get, but as a general rule, 87 octane fuel will be fine—just don’t go lower than that.

As long as we’re talking fuel, it’s always best to use ethanol-free fuel in equipment with small gas engines—if that’s not possible, nothing more than 10-percent ethanol. Ethanol can attract moisture, which will then separate and settle in the gas tank or carburetor, where it can corrode and clog the fuel system. For this reason, it’s also a good idea to treat gas with a fuel stabilizer.

Much like your lawn mower, generators need regular maintenance. However, since they often see less use, maintenance intervals tend to be farther apart. Typical maintenance would include changing oil, checking the air filter and changing it if needed, changing the fuel filter if so equipped, and checking the spark plug.

The best source of specific maintenance and troubleshooting information for your generator is the owner’s manual.

#6300. An elusive porcupine has a hidden glow that scientists just discovered

Researchers discovered that Mexican hairy dwarf porcupines glow under ultraviolet light, making them easier to spot at night.

The Mexican hairy dwarf porcupine is difficult to see in a tree even during the day. When ultraviolet light is shone on one at night, however, its quills glow a blue-green color.

This glow was observed on every live porcupine examined by a research team in southeastern Mexico. The researchers also used it to locate the animals in the treetops after dark.

Living animals also glowed far more brightly than old skins kept in a museum.

The team wrote that “no photoluminescence observations have ever been made in live individuals of the Mexican hairy dwarf porcupine.”

The study was carried out at El Colegio de la Frontera Sur (ECOSUR) in Chetumal, Quintana Roo.

Since 2023 the institution has helped environmental authorities to rescue and examine porcupines living in the city.

The Mexican hairy dwarf porcupine is a small spiny rodent that lives alone and is active at night. It spends most of its life in trees.

The species belongs to the same family as the larger North American porcupine. It is found from central Mexico to Panama, but little is known about its basic habits.

The first observation was made in June 2024 by senior author Jonathan Pérez-Flores. He was examining two females when he pointed a small ultraviolet flashlight at them and their quills lit up.

Ultraviolet light lies just beyond violet at the edge of human vision. Some materials absorb this light and release it again as a color that people can see.

The effect is known as photoluminescence. A similar thing happens when a white T-shirt is placed under a blacklight.

The flashlight used by the team also produced some visible purple light. For that reason only other colors such as green, blue and yellow were treated as a true glow.

Twenty adult porcupines were examined over the following three months. Seventeen of these animals were female and three were male.

Each porcupine was sedated for a health check. While it recovered in a quiet and dark place the light was held about a foot (30 centimeters) away.

Most of the photographs were taken with ordinary mobile phones.

All 20 animals glowed and this was true for both males and females. The head was the brightest region and showed a greenish-blue color.

The head also carries more quills than any other part of the body. The back, the legs and the tail showed the same greenish-blue wherever quills were present.

On the belly the glow varied in strength, which the team linked to the wider spacing of its quills.

Freshly collected quills told a more detailed story. Each one showed green where it looks yellow in daylight and blue at its brown tip.

Patches of skin without hair or quills did nothing more than reflect the purple of the flashlight. Neither the hair nor the claws glowed in any of the 20 animals.

The most unusual result came from the hands and feet of the porcupines. The palms and the soles of the feet produced a bright yellow glow that was visible from a distance.

“To the best of our knowledge, this phenomenon has not been reported in any other species of mammal,” the authors wrote. A 2023 catalog of 125 glowing mammals contains no such pattern, they noted.

Glowing has been described in a growing number of mammals, including domestic cats, pocket gophers and North American bats.

The source of the yellow glow on the palms and soles has not been identified.

The researchers suspect that pigments or proteins in that skin are involved but these were not tested in the study.

Two preserved porcupines from the ECOSUR museum collection were examined in the same way for comparison. Both specimens had been prepared more than 10 years earlier without the use of fluorescent chemicals.

In ordinary light the quills of these specimens had a pale cream color. Under ultraviolet light they gave off a greenish glow so faint that it could barely be seen.

No glow at all was observed on the skin or fur of the museum specimens. The palms and soles that had shone so brightly on the living animals also remained dark.

The authors suspect that the age of the specimens explains much of the gap. Keratin, the main material in quills as well as in human hair and nails, degrades slowly as the years pass.

Light could have made matters worse, since it destroys glowing molecules in keratin through a process called photobleaching.

This finding is relevant because the majority of studies on glowing mammals have relied on museum specimens.

Porcupines have been included in only a few of these studies and observations of live animals had been anecdotal.

The authors argued that “it is essential to conduct this type of research on both living and dead organisms to observe any differences.”

The authors cited a 2022 study that found green-glowing quills on museum skins of African porcupines but not American ones.

The researchers next wanted to know whether the glow had practical value, since canopy animals are hard to census.

For the test they chose trails on the ECOSUR campus where porcupines had been seen before. The route was walked twice a month from July to December 2024.

Every walk began no earlier than 7 p.m. and ended by midnight along roughly 0.6 mile (1 kilometer) of trail. At 10 stops spaced about 330 feet (100 meters) apart, the canopy was searched for 15 minutes.

Trees along the route stood 39 to 49 feet (12 to 15 meters) tall. Even so, the quills and soles stood out against leaves, bark and fungi.

Over the 12 walks, porcupines were detected 20 times, or roughly 1.7 sightings per route.

This porcupine is docile and can stay still for several minutes, so the animals found were photographed and filmed.

The authors wrote that “no previous study had used this method for locating arboreal mammals during nighttime surveys.”

The survey method does have an important limitation. Males and females of this species cannot easily be distinguished and individual animals lack any markings that would identify them.

For this reason the 20 sightings may not represent 20 different porcupines. The same animal could have been recorded on more than one night.

The photographs were also taken in a range of settings and mostly with mobile phones. Only three of the 20 sedated porcupines were male.

The function of glowing in mammals remains a matter of debate among scientists. Some researchers consider it a simple by-product of the pigments or structure of fur and skin.

Others prefer a checklist of five criteria drawn up by earlier researchers. Under it the glowing material should sit somewhere visible.

The animal should also live in conditions where the glow would show.

A third criterion asks for visual behaviors that might rely on the pattern. The remaining two deal with the wavelengths involved and with whether any onlooker has eyes sensitive to them.

In the porcupine’s case the authors believe the first three have been met. A related species, Coendou spinosus, presents its back and vibrates its quills when threatened. A glow could add to that display.

“Photoluminescent structures may facilitate perception and communication among individuals of this species during the night,” the authors wrote.

For the other two criteria the evidence is circumstantial. Many rodents may see ultraviolet light. Nobody has checked this porcupine for the light-sensing proteins, called opsins, that this would need.

Future research could test whether porcupines use the glow to find one another in the dark.

The flashlight used in the study emitted light at 395 nanometers and this appears strongly violet.

The team recommends that surveys also test ultraviolet light at a shorter wavelength of 365 nanometers, since some animals glow differently under each wavelength.

The study shows that a simple flashlight can help scientists find an animal that is otherwise very difficult to observe.

The full study was published in the journal Neotropical Biology and Conservation.

#6299. Trump says no Iran deal needed after conflict drove GOP’s midterm losses

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a Wednesday ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in honor of Veterans Day. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

The possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

Vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself said so last night."

Trump has said that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over."

Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president said Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!"

The situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

Trump, Vance and other administration officials have said in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

Trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday showed that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "quickly."

“Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers said in one campaign ad.

On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

As the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

“With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”

Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

Asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he said: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”

On Wednesday (Nov. 25), the distant ice giant Uranus will be at its best and brightest. Here's when, where and how to look for the seventh planet.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of the hardest planets to see in the solar system — the distant ice giant Uranus — reaches its annual opposition on Wednesday (Nov. 25), just a day after the Beaver Supermoon. It's the best time to see the seventh planet from the sun, but you'll need to use stargazing binoculars or a good backyard telescope to find it.

Uranus is faint, slow-moving and rarely a target for casual stargazers. However, on Nov. 25, and, for a few weeks on either side, it will be at its closest point to Earth this year and will appear at its brightest, making it possible to spot.

Opposition occurs when Earth passes between Uranus and the sun; Uranus will be "opposite" the sun, hence, "opposition." The moment of opposition will happen at 6 p.m. ET on Nov. 25, according to EarthSky. Consequently, Uranus will rise in the east around sunset, reach its highest point in the sky around midnight and set in the west around sunrise.

You can find it in the constellation Taurus, close to the Pleiades open star cluster, also known as the Seven Sisters and M45. Uranus will be a few degrees southeast of the cluster, appearing as a faint point of light, about two-fifths of the distance between the Pleiades and Aldebaran, the brightest star in Taurus.

At magnitude +5.6, Uranus is technically visible to the naked eye under very dark skies. However, binoculars or a telescope will make it much easier to find.

Uranus as seen by NASA's Hubble Space Telescope.

At opposition, Uranus will be 18.4 astronomical units (AU) from Earth — about 1.7 billion miles (2.7 billion kilometers) away. Through a telescope, it will appear as a tiny blue-green disk. Its color comes from methane in its atmosphere, which absorbs red wavelengths of sunlight.

Named after Ouranos, the ancient Greek god of the sky and the heavens, according to the Planetary Society , Uranus is one of the least understood planets in the solar system. A day on Uranus lasts for about 17 hours, and the planet rotates sideways, according to NASA. It takes 84 Earth years to orbit the sun.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Uranus also has 13 faint rings and at least 29 known moons, the most recent of which was found in 2025 by the James Webb Space Telescope. It was named Uranus XXVIII and orbits between the moons Ophelia and Bianca. Many of Uranus' moons are named after characters from the works of William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope.

The distant planet has been visited only once, by NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft on Jan. 24, 1986. However, contrary to what the probe found, scientists now think the planet emits its own internal heat. That could increase pressure on NASA to prepare a Uranus Orbiter and Probe (UOP), a mission concept the National Academy of Sciences recommended in 2022 as a high-priority planetary science mission for the next decade.

Uranus will next come to opposition on Nov. 30, 2027.

#6297. Exploding stars were supposed to free light from early galaxies, but they may have done the opposite

Hubble spectra of six young galaxies suggest winds from exploding stars trapped the light that drove the reionization of the Universe, rather than freeing it.

For most of its first billion years, the Universe was wrapped in a fog of hydrogen gas that blocked ultraviolet light. Something cleared that fog.

Astronomers have long assumed that exploding stars helped, by blasting open channels for light to get out of young galaxies.

New Hubble observations of six nearby galaxies point the other way: the galaxies leaking the most light were the ones whose stars hadn’t started exploding yet.

Cody Carr led the study as a postdoctoral scholar at Zhejiang University in China and is now a postdoctoral researcher in astronomy at the University of Michigan.

Renyue Cen of Zhejiang and Stephan McCandliss of Johns Hopkins University were the senior authors, and nearly 30 researchers from more than a dozen institutions took part.

“Basically, how these galaxies were leaking ionizing radiation isn’t what we thought,” Carr said.

In the early Universe, hydrogen atoms were whole, each a proton with an electron attached. Gas like that soaks up ultraviolet light.

High-energy light from the first galaxies eventually knocked the electrons off, and gas in that state is transparent. Astronomers call the change reionization, and Carr described it as the last major phase transition of the Universe.

The puzzle has been how the light got out, because a galaxy forming stars at a furious rate is also full of gas and dust that absorb that light.

One long-standing answer involved supernovae, the explosions that end the lives of the biggest stars. Their winds, the idea went, pushed the gas aside and opened the way.

The alternative is that the light escaped earlier, while the biggest stars were still alive. Their own radiation and the fast winds blowing off their surfaces would have done the work, before any star had exploded.

Galaxies from the early Universe are too faint and too far away to study in this detail, so the team picked six nearby galaxies that resemble them.

All six are compact and forming stars at a high rate, and all six have similar mass and chemical makeup. What differs is how much of their high-energy light escapes – from less than 0.4 percent to about 21 percent.

The team used the Hubble Space Telescope to take deep spectra of each one, spreading the ultraviolet light into its component wavelengths.

Gas moving toward us absorbs light at slightly shifted wavelengths, so the dips in a spectrum show how fast a galaxy’s wind is blowing and how much gas it carries.

The spectra also show how old each galaxy’s current burst of star formation is. The biggest stars live only a few million years before they explode, so a burst younger than about three million years has no supernovae yet.

The three galaxies leaking the most light were the youngest, with bursts under about four million years old.

In the youngest of all, the absorption came mostly from the fast winds blowing off massive stars, at around 6.7 million miles per hour (3,000 kilometers per second). The galaxy-wide wind was slow.

The three weakest leakers were older, and their spectra looked different. The stellar-wind signature had faded, and a galaxy-wide wind had taken over, carrying more neutral hydrogen and more dust.

In the youngest galaxy that wind moved at roughly 335,000 miles per hour (150 kilometers per second). The oldest galaxies drove winds about five times faster.

The faster the wind, the less light got out. The authors read that as the launch of a wind, driven by exploding stars, that sweeps gas and dust up into the outflow, where it blocks the light that had been escaping.

“It appears that energy input from supernovae has stirred up the surroundings and increased, rather than decreased, the coverage of neutral gas and dust that suppresses ionizing radiation escape,” McCandliss said.

The team checked whether the pattern holds beyond six galaxies. They stacked the spectra of 89 galaxies from a larger Hubble survey into three groups by how much light escapes.

The strongest leakers showed narrower hydrogen absorption than the rest, in line with slower winds, and the non-leakers hosted the fastest winds.

The timing changes the arithmetic of reionization. A galaxy’s contribution depends on how much high-energy light it makes and what fraction gets out, and those two things can peak at different times.

If the light escapes while the biggest stars are still alive and shining, galaxies like these could have done more of the work than models that wait for supernovae allow.

Simulations that explain reionization lean heavily on supernovae. Cen said the results point to a need to examine how radiation and winds from young stars shape the surrounding gas before the first supernovae explode.

Six galaxies is a small sample. The ages come from fitting models to the starlight, so the timeline is an average rather than a clock. Hubble’s spectra also can’t see the hottest wind gas, which only shows up in X-rays.

The team looked for X-rays from the strongest leaker with a separate telescope and found none. That fits a galaxy whose supernova-driven wind hasn’t started.

The six galaxies are also heavier and richer in heavy elements than the galaxies of the first billion years.

In lighter, more primitive galaxies, the authors expect radiation to matter even more. Massive stars there are likelier to collapse into black holes without exploding, which would delay the supernova winds further.

Whether compact galaxies like these were enough to clear the fog on their own is still an open question. Carr and his colleagues are seeking more Hubble time to observe more galaxies.

The 36-year-old telescope is near the end of its working life, the authors wrote. The proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory is one instrument that could take over this kind of measurement.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Astronomy.

In an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.

Grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” says Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”

Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.

Moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.

“My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz says. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”

#6294. Electrons usually flow freely through metals, but Columbia scientists just found a way to trap them in place

Physicists trapped electrons at a missing atom inside a metal crystal, where quantum interference left them no route out.

A metal conducts electricity because its electrons spread through the whole crystal, the way a ripple spreads across a pond rather than staying where it started. There’s nowhere in a metal for one to hold still.

However, in a palladium compound made at Columbia University, two of them hold still anyway, pinned to a single missing atom.

Morgan Thinel, Simon Turkel and colleagues in Columbia’s Department of Physics and Department of Chemistry found them with a microscope that feels a surface atom by atom.

Two of the authors also work at Brookhaven National Laboratory, and the group’s theorists reproduced both states on paper.

The trap is not a wall around the electron. It is the metal crystal’s own geometry cancelling every route out.

The material is Pd5AlI2, a palladium-aluminum-iodine compound that Xavier Roy’s chemistry group at Columbia built a few years ago. It is a van der Waals crystal, which means it comes apart into sheets the way graphite does, and the sheets stay metallic.

The compound’s electrons moved more slowly than anyone expected, and the group published the reason last year. Call it gridlock: an electron has competing routes to the next atom, and the routes cancel.

The cancelling is the whole mechanism here. A quantum particle does not take one path; it takes every available path at once.

The paths add up like waves, reinforcing in some directions and wiping each other out in others. When the wiping-out is complete, there is no route out at all.

Physicists call the result a bound state in the continuum. The particle is stuck in place even though it is surrounded by an unbroken range of energies into which it could escape.

Light does this. Over the past decade, engineers have etched patterns into materials to catch photons that way, and the trick now drives lasers and sensors. In a metal, it had stayed out of reach.

The team split a crystal open in vacuum and cooled it to about 7 degrees above absolute zero. Then a scanning tunneling microscope measured how easily electrons flow into the surface, point by point and energy by energy.

Across a clean stretch, the answer was much the same everywhere, which is what a metal crystal looks like. Over one kind of flaw in the lattice, two sharp peaks appeared. One sat 475 millivolts above the metal’s own energy floor and the other 620.

Comparing the images with simulations identified the flaw: a single palladium atom missing from the layer buried inside each sheet. Vacancies like it turned up across the crystal at roughly two trillion per square centimeter.

Both states hug the vacancy inside a single nanometer, a span a few atoms wide. A normal defect in a metal only nudges the passing electron waves. These two were not passing.

“Bound electrons shouldn’t occur in a metal, but they do in Pd5AlI2,” said Raquel Queiroz, a theoretical physicist at Columbia who built the models behind the result.

“What we have observed is the first clear evidence of quantum interference trapping a state in a metal.”

Mapping each peak across the surface produced two pictures. The lower one has four lobes, like a clover. The upper one is a plain circle.

Those are the shapes of orbitals around a single atom, which is an odd thing to find around an absence.

The team’s model is a stripped-down version of the layer with one atom removed. It produced both shapes, and put them a few hundred millivolts above the energy floor, where the microscope found them.

The circular one only appears once the model includes the iodine atoms sitting above and below the gap.

The team also answered the obvious objection. The gridlock in an idealized version of this lattice is perfect, and perfect conditions are not what a real crystal offers.

Loosening the model so the electrons are not quite frozen keeps the two states tightly bound across a wide range of settings, including the ones that match the real material.

When two palladium atoms were missing from neighboring sites, the pair of states became four. Each of the original two had split, into a slightly lower energy and a slightly higher one.

That is what happens when two atoms bond into a molecule. The resemblance runs even further. For the four-lobed state, the lower version piles electron density between the two gaps at 440 millivolts. The higher one, at 510, leaves the middle empty.

Move the vacancies two lattice spacings apart and the splitting disappears.

So the trapped states behave like the orbitals of atoms that are not there, and two of them nearby make something like a molecule out of two holes.

No one is placing these on purpose yet. Every vacancy here arrived by chance while the crystal was growing.

That is the sharpest difference from the light version of the effect, where the pattern goes exactly where the designer wants it. Roy’s and Abhay Pasupathy’s groups are working on putting flaws where they choose.

What a trapped electron is good for is also open. The authors note that photonic bound states have essentially unlimited lifetimes, and suggest these might carry charge without loss at their own energies, but nothing here measured current through one.

“And if you trap a particle, you can manipulate it,” Roy said. The uses he and his colleagues point to, from quantum sensors to quantum computers, are a long way past what was measured.

The prediction worth testing is that the lattice did this, not the material. If gridlocked hopping is the ingredient, other crystals with the same frustrated geometry should trap electrons the same way.

The authors name two common lattice patterns to look at next. That is a recipe, and the next paper either finds one or does not.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6293. Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage declared winner of open House seat

Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, fifth from right, joins incoming members Thursday for their freshman class photo on the House steps outside the Capitol. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once said he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

The Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

Dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

“Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, said in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”

LePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. He is one of three Republicans, along with Texas’ Jace Yarbrough and Tennessee’s Brent Taylor, to have flipped a House seat, although Maine’s 2nd District is the only one of the three that wasn’t redrawn to favor the GOP.

LePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent New England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

Golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

“I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden said in a social media post last week.

Dunlap initially launched his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.

#6292. Dams may be getting blamed for carbon emissions that would occur naturally

A global study suggests that conventional carbon accounting may substantially overestimate certain greenhouse gas emissions directly attributable to dams.

When a river is dammed, decomposing organic matter in the resulting reservoir can release carbon dioxide and methane.

That is why reservoirs now sit in national greenhouse gas inventories. It is also why some people question hydropower’s green credentials.

But much of the organic carbon carried into reservoirs would have decomposed naturally in rivers and estuaries even without dams.

A new study estimates that dams add about 21.5% to the emissions from the carbon they trap, once a free-flowing river’s own emissions are counted.

For the type of carbon tracked in the study, the net emissions attributable to dams were less than a fifth of conventional estimates.

The research was led by Wenqing Shi of Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology.

The co-authors came from the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, the University of North Carolina’s Institute of Marine Sciences, and Aarhus University in Denmark.

“High carbon emissions from reservoirs have sparked controversy over dams,” the team wrote.

In an interview with Earth.com, Shi noted that a fair test compares the same river with and without the dam, from the reservoir down to the estuary.

“We need to distinguish emissions that occur in a reservoir from emissions actually added by the dam,” Shi said.

Rivers carry about 940 million tons (850 million metric tons) of land-grown carbon to the ocean every year. Some of it decays in the channel on the way down.

Most of it settles in estuaries, where it decays too, releasing the same two gases.

A dam interrupts the trip. More than 70,000 large dams now stand on the world’s rivers, and each one catches carbon that would otherwise have kept moving.

The usual accounting charges every ton of gas rising from a reservoir to the dam that made it. That treats the carbon as if it would have stayed put without the dam.

Shi’s team ran the numbers both ways for 5,346 dammed reservoirs around the world: once with the dam in place, and once with the river flowing freely to the sea.

Methane traps far more heat than carbon dioxide, so the team converted it to a carbon dioxide equivalent, at 27.2 times the warming over a century. That put the two scenarios on one scale.

The two rivers look very different. In the free-flowing version, about 4.9% of the carbon decays in the channel and the rest reaches the estuary.

In the dammed version, 88.3% of the carbon arriving from upstream is caught in the reservoir, 0.5% decays in the channel below, and 11.1% makes it to the estuary.

Nearly every dam, 99.4% of them, raised emissions compared with the undammed river. The average increase was 21.5%, and the team’s uncertainty range runs from 8.3% to 32.6%.

The conventional method counts all reservoir emissions as the dam’s doing. Measured against it, the net effect is 18.6% of the old figure.

“We expected the baseline to matter, but the size of the difference was striking,” Shi told Earth.com.

Shi emphasized that the 18.6% figure covers only the land-grown carbon particles the study followed, not every source of reservoir emissions or hydropower’s whole carbon footprint.

“The emissions themselves have not disappeared; what changes is how much can reasonably be attributed to the dam,” Shi said.

Added up, the world’s dams release an extra 6 million tons (5.4 million metric tons) of carbon dioxide equivalent a year, by the team’s estimate.

Hydroelectric dams account for just over half of that, with irrigation dams next and flood control dams third.

Per ton of trapped carbon, hydroelectric dams add the least, 16.5% against more than 19.4% for every other dam type. They lead the list because there are so many of them and they drain such large areas.

A few dams even cut emissions. On rivers flowing from cool regions toward warm coasts, carbon held back in cold water decays more slowly than it would in a warm estuary.

What a dam changes most is which gas comes out. In reservoirs, slow water lets organic-rich mud pile up and run out of oxygen, and that is where methane forms.

Free-flowing rivers generally have more oxygenated conditions that are less favorable to methane production.

In the team’s model, methane’s share of the warming from decaying river carbon rose from 4.4% without dams to 22.8% with them, more than a fivefold jump.

“Reservoir conditions can favor methane production, so shifting decomposition upstream can still increase the climate impact, even after accounting for the no-dam baseline,” Shi said.

Reservoir depth and how long water lingers behind the dam were the strongest controls.

Shallow reservoirs and very deep ones both pushed emissions up, while reservoirs between about 65 and 260 feet (20 and 80 meters) deep held them down.

Shi said that spread is one more reason not to apply a single correction factor to every reservoir.

The model follows only one kind of carbon, the particles washed in from the land. It leaves out carbon in soil flooded when a reservoir fills, carbon dissolved in the water, and algae grown in the reservoir itself.

All three can add to a reservoir’s emissions. So the team called its 18.6% a conservative figure, and the true share pinned on dams could be higher.

Those other sources, and hydropower’s full life-cycle impacts, still have to be assessed separately, Shi said.

The researchers also treated all incoming carbon alike, though carbon from different watersheds decays at different rates.

No global dataset yet describes how a dam changes the flow of the river below it, so that effect is missing too.

“A priority is to make the estuary baseline more site-specific,” Shi said. That means measuring the carbon arriving, how much of it is buried or decays, and the gases that come off.

The team also wrote that any carbon accounting for a dam should run from the reservoir all the way to the estuary.

Until that happens, the figure in a hydropower plant’s carbon ledger depends on where the ledger decides the river begins.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.
